speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my statement today marks the second occasion on which I have provided Parliament with an overview of the three main elements of the national security system for which I am responsible.
These elements are security intelligence, security enforcement and protective security. As last year, my remarks will complement the release of a public report by the director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.
This statement and the public CSIS report form part of an effort by the government to provide Canadians with information about their national security system and about the threats that it works to counter. Together with the annual reports of the Security Intelligence Review Committee, not only ministers and parliamentarians but all Canadians are afforded a window on security intelligence issues.
Canadians receive daily from many points around the world reports of unrest and upheaval, witnessing a constantly changing geopolitical landscape. They want to know what their government is doing in constantly tracking world events for an evaluation of their possible effects on Canadian interests.
At the same time, they know that the cold war is over and that allies such as the United States with its vast intelligence and defence systems have in consequence begun a re-examination of their priorities.
I am keenly aware that here at home there are expectations for this government to adjust to rapid change and shifting circumstances. Being asked are questions such as: How is the Canadian Security Intelli-

April 1, 1993
Routine Proceedings
gence Service moving to respond to rapidly changing world circumstances and the emergence of new risks?
As I announced last year in this place, I asked the director of CSIS to prepare for me an assessment of how the evolving security environment might affect the service's mandate over time. The director was to consider future security intelligence needs, examine how the service ought to be structured to meet those needs and determine the resource implications of any recommended measures, mindful of the budget realities and the government's commitment to improve the efficiency of organizations.

The Director of CSIS has assigned this job to a working group. I would like to tell you about the findings of this group and the decisions I made accordingly.
The working group has requested the input from 28 departments on the security threats facing Canada in the years ahead.
The group has also called upon the expertise of CSIS by asking its employees for ideas on the best way to carry out the mandate of the organization.
Finally, the working group has conducted an in-depth analysis of resource requirements in the context of the budget realities and the situation of the intelligence community in 1993.

This analysis has confirmed that since the end of the cold war a progressive reduction of resources which are typically allocated to traditional counterintelligence services and operations which are quite labour intensive was warranted.
An analysis of the global security environment has presented the government with the opportunity to now make over-all reductions while ensuring that the security intelligence mandate has met an acceptable level of risk.
Therefore, the government is reducing the number of positions for CSIS from 2,760 to 2,465. That is a reduction of about 11 per cent. These reductions are being achieved primarily through attrition and by tight control of the staffing process.
As many may know, the government expanded the service's personnel complement in response to a very thorough review in 1987 which was carried out by an
independent review team led by Gordon Osbaldeston. This team found that the new service, bearing in mind that CSIS came into existence in 1984-1985, was understaffed and underfunded to meet the changing security intelligence demands of the government. I refer to the CSIS public report for an informative, detailed discussion of resource issues as they have evolved since 1984.
Equally important is that the director's review has identified a range of activities and best management practices that emphasize the importance of intelligence analysis and operational flexibility.
We in this House realize that forecasting is an imprecise art. I want to share the general long-term outlook for those areas of particular concern for national security. I want to make it clear that my number one consideration in directing the service and the RCMP in its national duties is public safety. Canadians expect no less.
CSIS projected five years ahead to identify the kinds of national security risk that we might face. The implications for Canada were examined with reference to the service's responsibilities to investigate threats associated with espionage, foreign influenced activities and politically motivated violence.
First, the nature of espionage will certainly change in years to come. Hostile intelligence services will be paying more attention to economic and technological targets. Although economic espionage is not new and existed regardless of the cold war, some countries will likely increase their efforts to obtain our considerable industrial and technological expertise the fast and cheap way.
I personally intend to do my utmost to ensure that Canada's economy does not suffer because others want to take unfair advantage and gain at our expense. As a result CSIS will continue to ensure the protection of information and assets of national economic significance through assessment of potential threats and warning to government.
In line with this responsibility, I am pleased to advise that the service has established a liaison program with the private sector to enhance understanding and awareness of the vulnerability of information to clandestine acquisition. I will continue to pay close attention to CSIS activities in this area. I wish to emphasize that the service's role in economic security is defensive; that is we play an advisory and precautionary role.
April 1, 1993

Our mandate is to monitor and advise on state sponsored economic espionage. CSIS does not and will not concern itself with private sector industrial espionage. This is strictly the responsibility of the private sector.
In the area of proliferation, this government's commitment to the promotion of international peace and security obliges us to monitor the deadly traffic in weapons and technology of mass destruction, particularly when Canada and Canadians are involved. CSIS will continue to play an appropriate role in that effort.
As we know from recent events, terrorists remain active in many parts of the world, some of them close to home. Canada is used regrettably for fund raising, procurement of weapons, planning and as a safe haven by a number of extremist groups. CSIS has a vital role in monitoring these activities, as does the RCMP in investigating and apprehending those who conspire to commit criminal acts.
Regrettably the continued existence of international state sponsored terrorism is a cause for concern to all states which follow the rule of law. The director's task force found no expectation that international terrorism would diminish. The recent bombing in New York City underlines the vulnerability of free and open democratic societies to terrorism.
Global trends, including growing movements in pursuit of ethnic nationalism in various regions of the world, the growth of religious fundamentalism and increasing ideological extremism among certain right-wing groups, clearly warrant continued vigilance by the service. As the Secretary-General of the United Nations has warned, the new danger that will appear is more state fragmentation. He notes that rather than 100 or even 200 countries in the world we may well see up to 400 countries by the end of the century.
Canadians are largely a nation of immigrants. It is our heritage to give refugees and immigrants the opportunity to build new lives. As Canada becomes home to more refugees and immigrants-almost one million have arrived here since 1987 and one million more by 1997-for-
Routine Proceedings
eign influenced activities and homeland quarrels are likely to be a growing concern.
Emigre populations in Canada may be coerced, manipulated or exploited by homeland based interests. By the same token, insurgent or terrorist groups may try to use Canada and the local expatriate population as a source of aid and comfort.
Nevertheless I have a responsibility to help ensure that old quarrels are not brought to Canada by those few newcomers who cannot leave behind the political violence of their homelands.
I should also note that we have recently amended our immigration legislation to strengthen its control provisions. These provisions will help authorities deal more effectively with potential threats from terrorists and violence-prone individuals seeking admission to Canada.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is an essential element of my national security mandate and it continues to be responsible for the protective security and enforcement of laws relating to security offences. The RCMP plays an extensive role in security enforcement with respect to the Security Offences Act and other laws but also in providing protective security to VIPs, federal properties, airports, embassies and missions.
CSIS works in close co-operation with the RCMP, ensuring the exchange of criminal extremism and terrorism information relevant to law enforcement. As Solicitor General it is my job to emphasize the continued co-operation between the two agencies.
On a personal note I would say that Director Ray Protti and Commissioner Norman Inkster have given me every assistance in my task as Solicitor General for the past two years. There is a good working relationship between the personnel of the two forces and specifically between Mr. Protti and Mr. Inkster. I believe the difficulties of the past are not our concern now.

To conclude, the national security system in Canada has demonstrated its impressive capacity to adjust and change in response to changing circumstances.
I think that the findings of the Director's working group and the ensuing decisions will be indeed the tradition of excellence in dealing with major national security issues.

April 1, 1993
Routine Proceedings
Other democratic nations have noticed how successful we have been and are now asking Canada for advice on balancing individual freedoms and effective national security measures.

In a discussion last year with the British Home Secretary I explained the Canadian experience with a new Security Intelligence Act and the Security Intelligence Review Committee process.
I have encouraged both the RCMP and CSIS to discuss with their eastern European counterparts how police and security agencies function in a democratic society. This is surely a sign of how the times have changed.
At home and abroad change is overtaking and transforming many things we once accepted as fixed and immutable. I want to assure Canadians that we are alert to the potential effects of change, and we are working to ensure the continued safety and security of Canadians through an effective national security system. I am confident that Canadians can continue to enjoy a degree of safety and security that places our nation in the ranks of a fortunate few in the world.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to respond to the Solicitor General's second annual statement based on the public report of CSIS.
The annual statement has evolved out of a process of review of security and intelligence, as the Solicitor General has indicated, that began a number of years ago and which culminated in the five-year review of CSIS by Parliament a couple of years ago. It is hoped that the annual statement and the annual public report of the CSIS director will add to Parliament's understanding of the role of CSIS in national security.
I want to point out, as I did last year and as I think should be pointed out for the next while, that Parliament's five-year review involved 117 recommendations.
I sat on the committee and, while it certainly was not our belief that the government would immediately adopt all 117 recommendations, all of us who participated in the committee were disappointed that at the end of the day
only one or two recommendations were actually formally adopted.
However, the government and CSIS have responded in other ways to those reports, not just the parliamentary report but others, and one of those responses is this annual statement which we all agree is constructive.
For the record I want to point out that the role of monitoring CSIS and other players in the national security field is a job that has been given to the Security Intelligence Review Committee. This is a body appointed by the government which reports to the House of Commons as it sees fit, but at least once per year. The other structure that monitors is the subcommittee of the House of Commons justice committee which monitors SIRC and the other players as best it can. I see the chairman of that committee smiling at me from across the floor today.
In any event, the task of monitoring our national security agency is not one that parliamentary systems have taken to easily. We hope that we have found some of the right tools and are doing the job properly.
I want to make reference to portions of the annual report as discussed by the Solicitor General. From our perspective in Parliament we invest large sums of money in gathering security intelligence from many perspectives, including counterintelligence and counterterrorism. I think all Canadians would agree that the moneys we spend on those functions are actually moneys spent as a kind of insurance policy which permits our country to adapt, respond and prevent certain types of occurrences that would be very negative to our public interest. I think by and large we are getting value for our money but our job in Parliament is to make sure that we get value for money. That is one of the focuses I bring to my remarks now.
One of the newer areas of concern and focus for CSIS and other elements of our national security establishment is economic security, the potential for theft of our economic secrets, our technologies, most of which is in private hands but some of which is in government hands. As the Solicitor General pointed out, the role of CSIS now is only to monitor, do surveillance and protect against economic thefts of the nature that are sponsored by foreign states.
April 1, 1993

Routine Proceedings
There are in existence all around the world many initiatives in the private sector where companies steal from other companies. At this point I do not believe that CSIS is authorized to chase those, but the Solicitor General has pointed out that CSIS is now liaising with elements of the private sector in an effort to make the private sector aware of the context of the risks, of the background of the players and of those against whom the private sector should be protecting itself. That is a useful taxpayer paid function.
However, not just in Canada but in other countries in the west there is now an issue being debated publicly as to how much the taxpayer should invest in protecting private assets and the technology of private companies. That is a legitimate concern. We have not fully debated or answered the question, but it is one that we, CSIS and the Solicitor General, will want to address in the months or years to come.
I want to point out what I believe may be omissions. I realize that the annual statements of the Solicitor General and the public report of CSIS will build year after year. We cannot knock off all issues in one sitting but there is one item of unfinished business that I will only make reference to, which is the Air India investigation that is still outstanding. Many Canadians are very concerned about that. We are awaiting a conclusion of the investigation and a decision by the government as to what will be done with the evidence it has accumulated on that situation.
Another omission to date, one that I hope will be dealt with in the future by the Solicitor General, is the security and intelligence operations and surveillance done by the Communications Security Establishment, known as CSE. That particular agency, while not under the jurisdiction of the Solicitor General, does gather intelligence information, electronic signals intelligence information. That has not as yet come under the proper ambit of this Parliament. We have not yet put in place procedures to monitor as we should.
I note that with the Supreme Court of Canada decision in Duarte and the provisions of Bill C-109 currently before committee and this House there may be occurring an inadvertent circumscription of the activities of CSE. Its electronic monitoring involving electronic signal surveillance, which is now done without warrant, may come under the ambit of Bill C-109. The comments of the Supreme Court of Canada in Duarte signalled that the state may not routinely monitor its citizens and invade their privacy without authorization or warrant. That is a matter that I know will come up in the future as well.
I want to raise another matter that I do not think the Solicitor General made reference to but which I am sure he would if I had placed it before him first, and that is we want to continue to remind CSIS to continue to be sensitive to Canadians bom in other countries who are now full-fledged Canadian citizens, particularly when incidents involving our national security arise. These people have to be treated as Canadians and not be assumed to be risks simply because they were bom in other countries.
There is a grey area here. I know that CSIS is aware of it. We have dealt with it at the national security subcommittee. I hope my remarks will encourage CSIS to be very vigilant and sensitive to the positions of these many Canadians as CSIS does its work attempting to deal with counterintelligence and counterterrorism within the context described by the Solicitor General.
I also want to acknowledge the staff reductions indicated by CSIS in the counterintelligence area. They are probably a function of the reduction in cold war intelligence battles that went on for many years. The need to engage in that whole round of activities with the former Soviet bloc is not as vital as it once was and may continue to diminish.
I hope those staff reductions would allow cost savings to the taxpayer. I am not so sure I saw it in the estimates. The budget appears to have continued on at the same level, notwithstanding the proposal to have staff reductions. It is hoped we can take a closer look at that issue at the subcommittee.
Finally I want to reconfirm for all of us in this House that the structures of the Security Intelligence Review Committee and the national security subcommittee will hopefully continue to do their jobs in monitoring our security and intelligence establishment in this country throughout the denouement of the cold war and this period of an apparent increased threat of terrorism emanating from the various conflicts around the world.

April 1, 1993
Routine Proceedings

Madam Speaker, as a member of the House subcommittee on national security I am pleased to respond to the minister's statement today with respect to his second annual report on the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. I thank him for giving me the information ahead of time. It came to my office late yesterday afternoon.
First I congratulate the minister on making an announcement that calls for a reduction in staff. Many of us on this side of the House over the past few years have been somewhat critical of the increase in the funding to CSIS, when other departments were being cut back at a time of restraint, and the proliferation of staff.
I realize a report was done a number of years ago by Mr. Osbaldeston that called for an increase in staff. We accepted that as having been necessary at that time. It is a good move at this point, now that the cold war has wound down or is winding down, to reallocate resources within the intelligence community and in doing so to find a way of actually reducing staff. I believe this mainly will be done through attrition and fortunately not through lay-offs.
The whole area of economic intelligence, espionage, counterespionage and so on is something, as the previous speaker and the minister have said, that has been with the world for a very long time. If we read about the historical antecedents of the intelligence world we find that it was essentially economic in the first place. As empires developed, governments felt they had to protect their foreign interests. Usually those foreign interests were economic and material. They were not so much political because the old trading companies controlled the monopoly on foreign trade. It was not really a government initiative in those days, although governments did open up avenues of exploitation through political processes and military processes.
The military intelligence and the economic intelligence went hand in hand to develop commercial empires. In effect we are actually returning, in a historical perspective, to some of the origins of the intelligence world.
The difference today is the obvious difference in technology. Quite frankly the minister, or any minister in his position, has a dilemma here.
It is one thing to say that the intelligence community, in this case CSIS, will liaise with the private sector. That is a duty. It has to perform that exercise. However it is much more difficult and confused to say this is where liaising ends and this is where participation begins in the process of protecting economic interests, in this case technology, technology transfer, research and development and so on.
Canada, along with the United States and western Europe, is a country that is on the leading edge in many of these technological fields so obviously we are prime targets.
I do not know how we can solve this problem. We cannot really solve it today or even this year because it is a growing problem. It is going to be an expanding problem. With high technology, computers, and information technology growing at such a rapid rate when government institutions such as CSE and CSIS become involved in finding out how they can protect Canadian economic, industrial and technological interests I am quite certain, just as certain as I am that I am standing here today, that will involve us somewhere down the road with active participation, not just passive.
That is the time that very serious considerations will have to be made and decisions taken. As the previous speaker said it involves taxpayers' money. We are going to have to ask the question: Should government or its agencies which are funded by taxpayers be out there gathering information to protect private sector technological developments, research and development and so on? This is something that cannot be codified today. It cannot be regulated because it is moving so quickly. The whole process is moving quickly.
I call upon the minister and his senior advisers in this area to keep a very close watch on how deeply CSIS, CSE and the RCM Police actually become involved in what I would consider a private sector problem, even though I would argue that the state has not only a right but a duty to protect economic interests in a general way.
Just to repeat myself for a moment, it is a very murky line. It is a very blurred area between liaising on one hand and actually, before we know it, becoming directly involved in the protection of private sector economic and technological secrets and so on.
April 1, 1993

That is an area to which we are going to have to give ongoing consideration. I would hope that the subcommittee of this House on national security and intelligence would have as one of its prime subjects over the next several years working with SIRC, the Security Intelligence Review Committee, and the minister and his staff on an ongoing basis.
The minister also made reference to international terrorism and the fact that Canada is used from time to time for fundraising for these various groups. The IRA is one glaring example, one hideous example, but there are several others.
Canada is also used as a haven, a safe house, for international terrorists. They can come here and sleep it off for a few days, a few weeks or a few months in relative peace and tranquillity. To say this is irritating is to put it mildly.
I recall that a number of years ago previous governments were warned that certain elements were coming in from Asia, that the Asian gangs were arriving in this country. I know it was extremely difficult to try to survey them, to try to investigate and determine who were legitimate refugees and who were gangsters, political thugs and so on.
The boat people are a very good example. Many of these people came in with no identification. There was no way to trace their origins or their country of nationality. Many of them were ethnic Chinese whom the Chinese authorities forced into North Vietnam in the 1960s. Ho Chi Minh did not want them.
When the Vietnamese war was over they flooded south into South Vietnam and joined the legitimate refugees, the boat people. Eventually they ended up here in Canada. A lot of these Asian gangs, Vietnamese, Chinese or from Hong Kong, have been coming into Canada with great regularity. We have not really made the effort we should have made to sort these people out, detain them and hold them until we are perfectly satisfied they are not members of these gangs.
I have made reference to Asian gangs. There are political and criminal undesirables from all over the world coming into our country. I am not saying they are coming into Canada in vast numbers, but we have to
Routine Proceedings
keep up our surveillance. This is where CSIS, along with the immigration department, plays a very important role.
If it takes longer then we should take longer to investigate these would-be refugees, or immigrants for that matter, if there is any doubt as to whether they are related to these gangs, political terrorist groups and criminal organizations. Quite frankly legitimate refugees and immigrants to this country and indigenous Canadians do not want that political and criminal riff-raff from the world coming to poison our society. We have to do everything we can to get a handle on this and to keep these thugs out of Canada.
There was another reference to the foreign nationalist political groups in the country. I realize that the world is in a flux right now. We are speaking of course of countries such as the former state of Yugoslavia, but there are many other examples. On the one hand we want to accept legitimate refugees. We want to give them a safe haven. We want them to come here because we know they will make useful, productive Canadian citizens and will add to the great cultural mosaic of our country. On the other hand, however, we have to be extremely vigilant in making certain that we are not setting up little nationalist political groups transplanted overseas in order to carry on the same nefarious activities they did back home.
The Liberal spokesperson just before me made a passing reference to CSE and Bill C-109. We finished the bill last night without amendment. I was chair of that committee and I will be presenting the report in a few minutes. I just want to say in passing that I sincerely hope that Bill C-109 will relate to the activities of CSE.
I would like to ask the minister, although he cannot respond at this time, if he would consider checking to see how that bill will impact on the Communications Security Establishment. CSE is such a secret organization. It has been extremely active without any parliamentary control, as far as the House of Commons is concerned at least, since its origin.
On the one hand I realize we need surveillance and increased technological surveillance in this highly technological age in which we live, but on the other hand the protection of private citizens' activities must also be considered as well.

April 1, 1993
Routine Proceedings
I am going to close on this last note, which is not in the report for obvious reasons. We appreciate what the minister had to say yesterday with respect to Leslie James Bennett who is now and has been for many years living in Australia. I am not going to go into all the details. The minister said yesterday in the House I believe that the government does not and never has considered Mr. Bennett to be a spy, a mole or disloyal.
I would ask the minister today in the House if he would seriously consider some kind of monetary recompense for Mr. Bennett. Mr. Bennett left this country in disgrace in the eyes of the public. Although he was innocent he lost his career and his family. He went to Australia to try to start a new life. He went, I believe, with a pension of $4,500 in 1972. To the best of my knowledge he has no other source of income or had no other source of private income at that time, and I do not believe he has to date. He sat there and suffered in the Perth area of western Australia all of these years trying to get redress.
The minister went a long way yesterday and I thank him for that. However, I call upon him now to try to come to some kind of monetary solution to assist this man. He is getting on in years and will not be living for that much longer. I believe he has lived in relative poverty all because he was under suspicion in an intelligence community that almost thrives on suspicion at times. I think he was dealt with by the RCMP and his superiors in a very unfair way.
I am happy to have responded to the minister's statement this morning. I look forward to the work of the House committee on national security and intelligence getting deeper into these issues that the minister has raised and that we have raised on this side of the House.

Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 34(1), I have the honour to present to the House, in both official languages, the report by the Canada-Europe Parliamentary Association of a meeting with the Council of Europe
Standing Committee on Agriculture, held in London, Middlesex, March 1 to March 4, 1993.
That meeting came as a direct result of a report given in this House by the association where we found that European parliamentarians in the main were not knowledgeable about Canadian policies and practices in areas such as agriculture, forestry, environment, et cetera, to the detriment of Canada in its world trading possibilities and things such as the GATT. It became apparent that a meeting of this order was necessary and 34 parliamentarians responded. It was a good opportunity.
I thank the government for its involvement. I urge the government and all parliamentarians to keep up the knowledge of Canada and express it around the world.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present the 81st report of the Standing Committee on House Management concerning parliamentary reform. If you will allow me, Madam Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on that report.
The report I am tabling this morning contains about 30 recommendations for parliamentary reform. It is the result of innumerable hours of work, discussions and compromises on the part of all members of the committee; it is also the result of the patience and efforts they have devoted to it over the last 18 months.

I would like to take a few minutes to acknowledge the special contribution of the members of the subcommittee on parliamentary reform who have participated since the beginning of the exercise in the fall of 1991.
I would like to mention the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, and my hon. colleague, the hon. member for Peace River who not only presided over the subcommittee's work but also chaired the committee for 18 months and steered its deliberation on parliamentary reform until the very end.
April 1, 1993



I would like to stress the tact and leadership of the hon. member for Edmonton Southwest who from November 1992 until last week has guided our work and, as committee chairman, skilfully piloted the project to a successful end. As you all know, the hon. member for Edmonton Southwest is Mr. Jim Edwards.

Finally I would like to give special thanks to our staff who worked with us during the whole process, our clerks, and in particular the outstanding support and drafting skill provided by Jamie Robertson, our research officer who rendered our task possible and our work feasible.
I have sat at many meetings and deliberations of the committee on House management on parliamentary reform. I would like to pay special tribute today to my colleague, the member for Peace River. Throughout the deliberations he led our discussions. He has been the lightning rod, if I can use that term, behind the work that has been done.
We are tabling today a report that will help streamline the work of the House of Commons. It will bring in several significant changes to the work of the House of Commons.

Therefore, it is with great pride and with gratitude towards all the members of the committee that I table this major and innovative report which I submit to the House today.

Madam Speaker, it is an honour today to present this bill, an act to amend the Criminal Code and the Customs Tariff.
The purpose of the bill is to prohibit the production, sale and circulation of cards and games of a violent nature and to prevent their importation into Canada.
I propose this legislation in response to the outrage many Canadians and many of us in this Chamber felt and still feel after hearing of the importation into Canada of the so-called serial killer cards and games and the production in the United States of those board games as well.
The minister of revenue has said that he would prohibit the importation of these products into Canada but his department told him that he could not under the present laws. Rather than wait for the government to amend the law to permit the banning of this offensive material I am proposing the appropriate amendments in this bill.

April 1, 1993

Madam Speaker, I have the privilege to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36 signed by hundreds of people within my riding of Surrey North.
The petition points out that the planned closure of the immigration office in Surrey and New Westminster will result in people having to travel to Vancouver to receive
service. There are severe processing delays at the Vancouver office. This is going to result in diminished service in spite of the fact that the office in Surrey took in over $4 million in fees last year.

Madam Speaker, I rise to present a series of petitions in memory of all children who have suffered from the hands of others.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tremblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to begin the debate on third reading of Bill C-92, which amends the Income Tax Act and various other laws.
This bill will implement some important measures announced for the first time in the 1992 budget. It follows up an important promise made by this government to reduce spending so that we can lower taxes and
Government Orders
promote growth and competitiveness. This bill also includes some technical changes to the Income Tax Act.
These technical changes are the result of constructive comments we received from taxpayers and their advisers in recent years. The purpose of these changes is to maintain and increase the fairness and efficiency of the tax system. This is an important element of this government's commitment to strengthen the Canadian economy by eliminating barriers and distortions in the tax system.
Let me first of all discuss the proposed tax reductions.
Above all, Bill C-92 would assure legislative approval of the reduction of 1 per cent in the surtax on individual income which took effect on July 1, 1992 as well as the additional reduction of 1 per cent which took effect on January 1, 1993. With these measures announced in the February 1992 budget, the surtax falls to 3 per cent of basic federal tax; 14.6 million Canadian taxpayers will benefit from these reductions. The total impact of federal revenues is expected to amount to $6.6 billion over the period from 1992-93 to 1996-97.1 should point out, that these reductions are being covered by cutting expenditures elsewhere in government.
In addition, the House is being asked to consider a number of changes in the tax treatment of Canadian businesses. We propose to reduce the tax rate on income derived by corporations from manufacturing and processing from 23 per cent to 21 per cent, in two stages. The first decline takes effect on January 1, 1993. The second one, a one point reduction, is scheduled for January 1, 1994.
The goal of these initiatives is to assist companies in the manufacturing and processing sector as they restructure their operations and take advantage of new opportunities. This legislation also implements a number of other tax measures announced in the February 1992 budget.
The Income Tkx Act will be amended to no longer provide the $100,000 life-time capital gains exemption on real estate purchased after February 1992. The exemption will apply only to real estate purchased before March 1992.

April 1, 1993
Government Orders
The rules concerning labour-sponsored venture capital corporations are amended to increase the maximum credit for investments in these funds, increase the size of the company in which the funds may be invested and relax the eligibility criteria for the fund sponsorship.
The Income Tkx Act will also be amended to implement the Home Buyers' Plan. This measure allows homebuyers to withdraw up to $20,000 in existing funds from registered retirement savings plans and to use the money to finance the purchase of new or existing homes. Where the home is being occupied as the buyer's principal residence, there is no tax on the withdrawal. So far, there have been 130,000 withdrawals since the plan was announced.
The tax system will be modified to treat common-law couples in the same way as married couples. The broader definition of "spouse" that is currently used in the Income Tax Act for provisions relating to pensions and other retirement plans will be extended for all other purposes under this act. Under this broader definition, the term "spouse" will include both married and common-law spouses.
After discussing the measures in this bill that were announced in the 1992 budget, I would now like to return to some of the technical amendments we are proposing to the Income Thx Act.
First of all, we propose to reverse the ordering of the credit currently provided for the large corporations taxed in the special Part VI tax on financial institutions against the corporate surtax and income tax. This will allow foreign parents of Canadian companies to obtain recognition abroad for a larger portion of the Canadian taxes for which they are liable and provide an added incentive for them to continue investing in the Canadian economy.
Second, we propose to amend the Income Tax Act so that once the bill is enacted, the government can collect a portion of the taxes in cases where there is a dispute. This provision will apply only to disputed taxes of companies that are liable to the tax on large corporations. Individual taxpayers and small companies will not be required to pay over disputed taxes until a court has ultimately ruled on the question of liability of those taxes.
Finally, we are proposing certain changes to the 21-year rule for trusts. When the capital gains tax system was introduced in 1972, the then Minister of Finance said
it was necessary to tax cumulative gains at the time of decease, to prevent perpetual deferment of income tax and indefinite deferment of capital gains tax through the use of long-term trusts. One of the measures introduced for this purpose was the 21-year rule. This rule provides that the value of trust assets be determined every 21 years, beginning in 1993, and that any accrued capital gains on the assets in the trust at that time be taxable.
However, the 21-year rule had some flaws. Trusts were able to avoid the application of that rule by transferring trust assets to a newly created trust, thus benefiting from a new 21-year period. Moreover, the legislation then did not recognize that the conditions applicable to certain trust arrangements did not allow the distribution of trust assets to beneficiaries before the end of the 21-year period.
The proposed changes were initially announced on February 11, 1991. A provision will ensure that the 21-year period cannot be renewed through the rollover of trust assets to new trusts; in other words, it will no longer be possible to start from the beginning again and thus avoid the deadline set by the 21-year rule.
The second change will extend, for eligible trusts, the 21-year period, that is the date for reporting capital gains which have been accrued but not realized. We proposed this change so that the capital gains tax consequences will be essentially the same whether individuals give property directly to their children or to trusts for the benefit of such children.
Some members of the opposition suggested that the rich can avoid paying taxes by setting up trusts. This is simply not true. When assets are transferred to a trust, the accrued capital gains on those assets must be reported at that time.
Moreover, trusts or their beneficiaries are taxed each year on the income of the trust, just like any other taxpayer. The capital gains realized on assets held in a trust are treated as accruing to the beneficiaries of the trust, thus taking into account the legal reality of these arrangements.
In spite of the fact that the proposed changes to the 21-year rule prevent the indefinite rollover of taxable gains, they have been perceived as a giveaway. Nothing could be further from the truth.
April 1, 1993

I want to make it clear that trusts are not designed to be tax evasion schemes. They mainly serve to ensure the orderly transfer of assets in a family planning context. This concept should pose no problem to the members of this House, in that parents must be allowed to distribute their assets to their children and other heirs as they see fit.
The proposed changes will ensure that each generation will pay its fair share of tax on the accumulated wealth.
Madam Speaker, as you certainly know, an issue was raised in committee concerning proposed changes to the provisions of the Income Tkx Act on the confidentiality of taxpayer information. The issue has to do with the implementation of these arrangements and of the proposed changes for Revenue Canada employees.
This issue has already been brought to the attention of the senior managers of Revenue Canada by the Privacy Commissioner, Bruce Phillips. I have here a letter from Mr. Phillips in which he indicates that he is confident that the proposals can be integrated in a regime which will adequately protect the right to privacy of these employees.
In conclusion, the tax measures announced in the February 1992 budget, including those being implemented through this bill, are part of this government's action plan to set up an economic program supported by Canadians from all regions of the country. This plan includes measures to stimulate economic activities through personal income tax reductions, measures to stimulate the construction industry through the Home Buyers' Plan and measures to promote productive job-creating investments.
The bill also includes necessary technical amendments to the tax system.
In view of the above and in the interest of all Canadians, I urge the members of this House to support Bill C-92.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak against the passage of Bill C-92 and against this government.
Government Orders
The people of Canada have to realize this is a bill to implement measures brought forward in the February 1992 budget. That was over a year ago. Pray tell why it would take over a year to bring forward measures that were to be implemented in 1992.
The bill was introduced for first reading on November 26, 1992. It took a full 10 months for this government to move on this major tax bill. In England, when a budget is brought down, the bills implementing the measures in the budget are introduced almost simultaneously.
Why would it take 10 months for this government to bring forward this bill when it claims it is such a wonderful and terrific package? That is the first question I asked. Is it because the government could not ram it through its bureaucrats? Is it because this government was trying to be devious and bring forward measures in this package that were not particularly good for the people of Canada, along with some that were? It was a way of making the people forget and taking the heat off some things contained in this bill. It galls me to see some of the ways this government treats Canadian taxpayers, Canadian people.
It has taken 10 months to bring forward this bill. We had first reading on November 26 and second reading on February 23. Then we were in a big hurry of course. We had to hurry it through the committee. We had to rush and get everything all set up, because the government has to have this bill now. Now it is really urgent. The government has an opportunity to bring in closure, shut off debate and try to stop any kind of opposition there might be to some of the measures contained in this bill.
One of the things that happened particularly galls me. I was on the committee studying this bill. There was a clause in it having to do with personal tax returns. Frankly to this day I am not convinced whether the government was right in bringing forward this measure or not. I do know there was a lot of fear at the snooping powers that particular provision was giving the supervisors and employers of tax data employees about their personal tax information.
At committee stage that particular clause was removed from the bill. I have some press clippings here. At the time it sounded quite good. It said: "Ottawa drops plan to boost tax man snooping powers". One has to realize

April 1, 1993
Government Orders
this happened on March 23. Opposition MPs and the committee convinced the government that the Public Service Alliance of Canada had raised sufficient concerns to warrant deletion of this clause. There was no debate on this clause and it was deleted from the bill.
Lo and behold, report stage started on March 29 and the clause was reintroduced completely as is. There was no debate on whether it should be there or not. Just ram it through.
This government believes in top down democracy. It is its way or the highway. That is why the people of Canada are so disgusted with what is happening here. They feel so left out of any debate or any kind of consultation. They feel they cannot get their opinions through.
If we feel that way how can the people of Canada not feel that way? It is absolutely the most despicable, duplicitous way of behaving. It carries on and on.
I have to oppose this bill on the grounds that this government is doing things with this bill that are absolutely wrong for large numbers of Canadians. On the other hand, being as duplicitous as it is, it does things and proposes things in this bill which are quite good. Actually,the government has things in this bill we have asked for. It is its way of playing the political game so it can go to Canadians and say: "Look at those terrible Liberals; they oppose everything we do, even when it is things they have asked for". The government plays its crazy political games with the lives of Canadians and that is absolutely, unequivocally wrong. I do not want to be a party to this kind of deviousness.
It continues. Look at the newspapers today and pick out some of the headlines about the way this government operates. This headline is dated today, April 1, from The Ottawa Citizen and states: "Tories Force Vote on Free Trade Bill". We all know the U.S. is probably not going to move forward on this North American free trade bill. There is no rush for us here because there are a number of areas in the negotiations that have not been clarified and should be reworked. There are parallel agreements that have to be brought in.
Are the Conservatives interested in hearing what the Canadian people are saying? Absolutely not. They would not hold any hearings if they could get away with it, but they will not get away with it.
I must remind the Canadian people that second reading of the NAFTA bill occurred during one-half of a short day, which was yesterday afternoon. That is a very limited number of hours of debate on an extremely crucial piece of legislation that the people of Canada are very worried about. They have suffered from the effects of the free trade agreement which this government also rammed through without regard to the kinds of programs that-

Madam Speaker, I would point out to you that there is no government member in the House while we are studying a money bill. I think that is unacceptable. I ask you therefore to take a quorum count.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must take a moment to thank the member for Longueuil, because I did not realize there were no Conservative members in the House during my speech. I know that they do not like to hear what I have to say because I denounce these Conservatives who use the people of Canada and try to put things over them that are not good. It is called pulling a fast one. I know that they do not like to hear such things, but one of the reasons we are here is to represent Canadians and listen to them and do what is good for them, not the Conservative Party.
Excuse me if my language is a little strong, Madam Speaker, but it is disgusting to think that the Conservative Party's coffers are full-I must say that I cannot get over it. It angers me and all Canadians to think that Canadians' pockets are empty but the Conservative Party's coffers are full to overflowing.
That sends a message to people. Who is being served here? Is it the Conservative Party or Canadians? With all I see now and all that has gone on, I wonder if the people of Canada have been well served by this Conservative Party. If they do not like what I am saying, then they should do something, but they should listen.

I have news for the members of the Conservative Party. Canadians know what they have done and they understand it. This particular bill is a classic example of what they do continuously. They pretend to give with one hand to ordinary Canadians when they really are not. They are just looking after a few of their rich friends and that has to stop.
I have a feeling this Conservative government has been doing things to further the cause of the Conservative Party and not the people of Canada. I believe it is time we started representing those whom we have been elected to represent and that is average Canadians. It is essential.
Madam Speaker, you are going to say: "Well, maybe Liberals in the past were not that great". That bothers me because I have often heard a lot of accusations. As you know I have only been a member of the House of Commons since 1988. The other day I was in this House and questioned one of my colleagues who has been a member of Parliament for 25 years. I wondered if it is because I am in opposition. Is this a disease that happens to governments in power? It worries me because I know we will form the next government and I want to make sure we do not succumb to a disease such as that. I want to make every effort to make sure I do not succumb to that kind of disease.
I asked the member of Parliament who has sat as a Liberal for 25 years: "Was it that way when we were on the government side? You were there, tell me".

This is coming from someone else. I do not know but I hear the Conservative government saying that it is going to reform the institution of Parliament. Believe me, the only way to reform this institution of Parliament is to get

rid of this Conservative government because it does not know what it means to have democracy. It does not know the definition of democracy.

It does the same thing in every other thing it deals with. These are all today's headlines. This is again in the The Ottawa Citizen of April 1, 1993: "Tory slams PCs 'shirking' lobby review".

At a single stroke about 20,000 taxation employees will lose a right of privacy guaranteed to every other Canadian: the right to keep their financial affairs confidential. speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to see that we again have a large number of Conservatives in the House of Commons to listen to my sage advice. However, let me remind the Conservatives on that side of the House that we are opposed to this bill. It is not our responsibility to have and maintain quorum and to have a large number of members here. It is their responsibility to have their members sitting in this House to ensure that this piece of legislation passes. They claim they absolutely have to have it and that is why they imposed closure. They hold it near and dear to their heart.
I have a feeling that these people are embarrassed by some of the things they are doing and therefore it is veiy difficult to sit in the House and be told that this is not a good way to proceed. I would ask them to continue
sitting here and I will try to limit my speech to the content of this particular tax bill.
I will speak to the 21-year rule on trusts. We have heard a lot of things from this government on the reduction of debt and deficit. We have heard ad nauseam how great it was at reducing the debt and deficit. We all know that it does not know how to do it because the debt and the deficit are extremely large and it has been running this country for almost nine years. Obviously its talk is cheap. Its actions are what we have to watch.
Look at what is happening with the almost indefinite extension of the 21 years. Look at when capital gains were introduced. We have to remember that prior to 1972 capital gains or appreciation in value of any assets, whatever they were, were not taxed. When that was brought in it was decided that because trusts in essence never die-they are not human-there should be a way of taxing the capital gains held in them. At that time it was felt that 21 years was really a reasonable time.
Let me remind this House that this particular extension of the 21-year rule is extremely important to those trusts that were already set up prior to 1972. Remember that these assets have never had any kind of capital gains taxation. These assets, many of which are very large, have been held in these trusts for longer than 21 years but there has been no deemed realization. The only way not to have capital gains at this time, if they wished to avoid them, would be to distribute the assets to the beneficiaries. However, it is far better for those people who control those trusts to keep them as is.
This government has decided that these people would be allowed to defer taxation on the capital gains held in those trusts almost indefinitely. It is saying that they will be taxed some day. Yes, they will be taxed some day. We do not know when exactly. However, we do know that any kind of a tax deferral is generally a benefit. It is a huge benefit if it is deferred for a year, but if it is deferred for 50 years many things can happen and many laws can change. In essence it is as if there is no taxation on that for a very long time. This government that needs those tax dollars is saying: "We are going to allow them
April 1, 1993

not to pay taxes now on capital gains in those trusts for perhaps another 30 or 40 years".
When we were in committee we asked the finance officials if they could give us any kind of an estimate. Of course they could not. I have said this before. I have never heard of financial officials who could not give us an estimate on whatever it is they wanted. I am convinced that there are some facts and figures somewhere that would give a ballpark figure of the kind of tax revenues that are being forgone for the immediate and maybe the next 20 years. I think they are very substantial.
I want to believe when this government goes down to defeat that this will be seriously looked at and that this exemption will perhaps not be allowed to sit as it is being proposed today. It is a serious matter. The debt and deficit of this country are serious matters. Trusts by and large are a tax shielding mechanism.
I want to denounce this particular part of that bill. It has been trying to bring this in, trying and trying to bring this in. I will say that it is going to do it by ramming it through and not letting too much debate go on. It thinks the Canadian people are going to forget about it because there are good things in this bill and things that they might want. As usual the government carries on doing what it wants at the expense of ordinary Canadians.
It brings to mind what is happening in another area and that concerns the poverty line. A committee of this House is being boycotted by all opposition parties. The Tories do not like the statistics on poverty in Canada. They do not like the sheer numbers they see and have decided to redefine what it means to be poor so that they can have statistics that will favour them more.
How horrible to think that rather than address the real problems of joblessness and hopelessness, they would change the definition of poverty to suit their ends. How low can they go? I hope they cannot go much lower than they are going now and I hope it does not last much longer.
I wait, and I know that Canadians wait, to have an election so that they can voice their opinions and let the politicians know just how much they have had it with
Government Orders
their policies, with their lack of consideration of ordinary Canadians.
Another section of the bill concerns the taxation of capital gains, the $100,000. We know that capital gains exemptions were brought in by this Conservative government. We also know that by and large it is mostly wealthy Canadians who have been able to take advantage of the exemption on capital gains. The government told us that the excuse for bringing in the capital gains taxation exemption was to allow more investment in business.
We also know, we have the facts and figures to prove it, that it actually did not generate anywhere near the kind of investment in business that the government thought it would, not even one-half. I believe it is in the neighbourhood of perhaps $6 billion, but we know that it cost the government in tax revenues $20 billion and up. Those figures go back to perhaps 1991.
Now the government has decided it really should get out of capital gains exemptions, but rather than make a decision and treat all Canadians the same, it has decided to pick on one segment of society. It happens to affect those who can least defend themselves. It almost appears as if the government does it on purpose, attack those that cannot defend themselves. We see it over and over again.
Who does it attack? It attacked the seniors back in 1984-85 but, lo and behold, the seniors were better organized. They fought back and the government had to backtrack.
Just this year, at a time of total despair in the Canadian work force, we know the loss of jobs has been monumental. We know the unemployment rate is extremely high. We know those who have jobs are worried about keeping their jobs. We know those who have jobs have to work twice as hard as they have ever worked before just to make sure they can produce. We know all of that. Yet this government decides it is going to try and blame the woes of this country on the unemployed. It is going to try to make Canadians believe that large numbers of Canadians quit their jobs and go on holidays.
I do not know very many Canadians who quit their jobs these days because if they leave a job without really good reasons they are not going to get another one, and living on unemployment insurance is not the way most Canadians want to be.

April 1, 1993
Government Orders
Again the government is picking on those who really cannot defend themselves or have a difficult time defending themselves. When we look at the $100,000 capital gains we know that once again it is using the excuse that it wants to keep capital gains exemption taxation for those people to invest in business. Does a person who builds a small apartment building and who works very hard not contribute to the well-being of the business community in this country? I believe he does.
In Ontario the NDP has done everything in its power to kill the small investor. That is a shame. These people work very hard and perhaps have built a duplex or a small apartment building for income for their retirement. It is their retirement insurance. They have mostly built it themselves, maybe using small subcontractors. Maybe they bought an old house and converted it. If any capital gains at all is to be made by these people they are going to be hit by the federal government.
When I introduced the motion my feeling was that we should consider whether we want to have capital gains exemptions in the tax system. Perhaps we should not have them. However we should not pick on one group that tends to be the most defenceless versus the other, the friends of the Conservatives, the Bay Street boys, the brokers. If they make a gain because they have gone to their broker and played the stock market, that is all right. If they have not taken their 100,000 capital gains already, they can still use it.
I find it despicable that we play this kind of game with the ordinary people of Canada. It has to stop. That is one of the reasons I am totally opposed and will not support this bill even though there are measures in it that I support.
I know that in the past this same Conservative Party, when the Liberals had tried to bring in a many faceted tax bill, caused the bells to ring in this House for two weeks non-stop until the Liberals broke the bill apart and agreed to present it in different sections. That is what should happen to this bill.
Of course the Conservatives being in power have changed all the rules. Now members of the opposition have very few ways of delaying or stopping anything that goes through this House. What is happening here is by and large the death of democracy. The committee system does not work the way it should work, not if we look at
what is happening with this bill and what the committee did. Then the government turned around and reintroduced it as is.
That should send a message to people. Those members do not care. They just want their way no matter. They are told. It does not matter what kind of information is brought forward they choose to ignore it and go on to impose their will on average Canadians.
I want to stress that this bill contains some measures that if they were not passed would help bring down the deficit. They would help bring down the deficit this year. Perhaps we could then be somewhat closer to reaching the deficit targets that have been set previously. We could come somewhat closer.
Every year the government tells us in its budget that it is going to have these wonderful reductions in the deficit. It never happens. It does not happen if measures such as these are brought forward.
I beseech you, Madam Speaker, to let me address the people on the other side. Let me tell them that for all that is sacred in this democratic country and for all that we are facing serious financial problems, to delete that section of the bill. The government cannot allow these trusts to go on for another 20, 30, 40 or 50 years without getting the capital gains taxation, without those revenues which could help fund this debt and deficit. If the government does not want to use the money against the debt and deficit, perhaps it could use it to create some jobs, to do some of the infrastructure programs, to help Canadians get back to work and to help those in red despair in this country.

Madam Speaker, I might begin by telling the hon. member for Sudbury who just spoke that the Conservatives did not ring the bells on an income tax bill. They rang the bells back in the spring of 1982 over an energy bill. It was an omnibus energy bill that prompted them to act in that way. It had nothing to do with income tax.

April 1, 1993

In any event there are a number of things I would like to say at third reading on this bill and some of them relate to the hon. member for Sudbury, particularly with respect to the question of trusts.
The member said, and quite rightly, that the government acts as if it does not expect the Canadian people to notice what it is doing and that it assumes it can get away with certain things. Extending the capital gains tax exemption for these trusts was one of the things that it thought it could get away with.

At second reading of this bill, when I was making the very same arguments that she made this afternoon, she was on her feet siding with the government. She was saying that the NDP were making a big deal out of nothing and that she was thankful to the minister at that time for clarifying the matter. The best face that I can put on it for the Liberal Party is that some of them are teachable or that the hon. member for Sudbury was taking the party line on second reading and, to her credit perhaps, was persuaded in committee that the Liberal Party position on this, which was one of silence and collaboration, stunk and that maybe she should do something about it. The issue of trusts was the main thing. We did succeed, and this happened because the NDP requested it, in having some witnesses before the committee with respect to the 21-year tax exemption for trusts. We had some excellent testimony from Professor Neil Brooks and from Mr. Sidney Goldstein, a practising tax lawyer.
It was interesting to watch because by the time the witnesses finished not only had the hon. member for Sudbury seen the light but the members on the government side had been quietened. Their former exuberance, their former uncritical defence of this measure was silenced. Even the member for Mississauga South, and it is hard to imagine, seemed to be a bit on the quiet side by the time the witnesses got through explaining just what a real tax benefit this extension is for all the people who will be affected by it.
The Revenue Canada officials who appeared tried to argue that there is no tax benefit in trusts, no tax advantage. Amazing. People go to all the trouble of setting up these trusts for nothing, just because they like trusts. In some cases they may set them up in order to maintain control over certain assets, et cetera, but they certainly also do it because there is a tax advantage to be had. This tax advantage is extended and made more offensive by the measure that is before us in Bill C-92.
I am glad, even though we have not succeeded in defeating Bill C-92, that we have played a role over the last year or so in making sure that Canadians actually do know just what is going on here.

Had we not raised this, and for that matter had I not raised it as the NDP tax critic over the last several months, it would have just happened and it would have continued to have been what I called it once in this Chamber: a dark dirty secret about what the government was doing for the rich in this country.
It is not a secret any more. It is not as widely known as I would like, but it is not a secret any more. The government will have to answer for this. It will have to answer for the lie that this gives to its rhetoric about deficit reduction. How are ordinary Canadians to believe that the government is serious about deficit reduction when it sees that in spite of its rhetoric about deficit reduction it persists in maintaining and extending certain tax loopholes for wealthy Canadians?
If it was willing to close these loopholes and then say that it has closed a lot of these loopholes, closed them all, and its back is still to the wall fiscally then all this rhetoric about tough decisions might have some credibility. In the absence of that action that kind of rhetoric does not cut it with ordinary Canadians, even though they might be concerned about the deficit, as we all should be. People want to know that if governments are going to address the serious question of deficit reduction they are going to do it in a way that is fair, that calls upon everyone to sacrifice according to their means, and that does not exempt certain classes of people from contributing their fair share to the over-all common good.
That is what we have here. Certain classes of people are being exempted. In the meantime the poor are getting poorer and the middle class, as an hon. member said in this House the other day, is getting the shaft. That is certainly the way the people in my riding feel. They feel they are the people who are paying the bills in this country, who are obeying the rules in this country, who do not expect any special favours from government, who are working and contributing to their community, raising families, and going to work every day. Their income tax is coming straight off their cheques. They do not have any fancy pants lawyers and accountants to figure out how not to pay taxes.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to stand to ask a question of the NDP member. He said I thanked the Minister of Finance for clarifying his position when he spoke to this bill and explained how trusts were taxed and just exactly how the laws were applied. I did thank him because I was about to clarify it as well.
I have seen householders going out that were totally, grossly wrong and misleading. They were actually telling the people in different ridings in this country that trusts paid no income tax whatsoever and that is false.
I was pleased that the government was also on the track of making sure it understood what trusts were all about because it had absolutely no idea.
I can say once more that trusts do pay taxes at the top marginal rate on any earned income within that trust. If they have Canada Savings Bonds they pay the top tax rate on whatever interest is earned, so I had to clarify
that.
I also want to know whether the NDP members now understand that this was about capital gains and appreciation of assets that have been held in trust.
When I spoke at second reading on this bill I did state that I wanted more information. I wanted to know the rationale behind what the government was proposing to do because I like to be informed before taking violent stands one way or the other.
I did not get the information I was seeking from the Conservatives. I did not get the facts and figures. The information I did get led me to believe this would be very unfair and we actually need the tax revenues now and not 20 or 50 years from now.
Has the NDP finally learned what is in trusts and what it all means? I want to know this because it is essential. If it wants to pretend it knows how to run the economics of this country, it had better be informed.

Madam Speaker, we understood from the very beginning the difference between income tax and tax on capital gains.
I challenge the member to produce a householder or anything from any member that says these trusts pay no income taxes, because that was not what was said.
We were saying these trusts paid no capital gains tax and it was to have been paid at the end of the 21-year period that existed from 1972 to 1993. They paid no tax in that 21-year period. They were expected to pay tax at the expiry of that 21-year period and they were now not going to have to pay tax after the expiry of the 21-year period.
The hon. member may have been offended by some of the estimates that were used, but they were received from one of the witnesses whom she quoted in this House. I wish the hon. member would make up her mind. The only information we have been using when critcizing this is estimates given to us by the very same witness the member has quoted herself in this House, Professor Brooks.
If the hon. member is intent on exposing this, I do not know why she would try to muddy the waters by making false accusations about what the NDP has been saying about this.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member a question. It relates to his last point, which I do not think he had time to complete.
It concerns the use of people's income tax returns, which is a major change in this legislation. I want to refer him to the fact that the final change in this bill is quite different from what was explained in the standing committee. I do not know whether he or the Public Service unions have picked it up.
I just want to read it for him very briefly. It says:
-taxpayer information solely for a purpose relating to the
supervision, evaluation or discipline of an authorized person -
employed-to assist in the administration or enforcement of this
Act, the Canada Pension Plan or the Employment Insurance Act -
It includes all the employees of Employment and Immigration Canada and Health and Welfare Canada who deal directly or indirectly with Canada Pension Plan, as well as the employees of Revenue Canada. I spent

three years as a law clerk in a provincial legislature just reading bills. I know what is in the bill.
This has now expanded to three government departments. All these federal government employees will now be supervised and evaluated by their income tax returns. That is what is in the bill. Do not tell me it is not in the bill because I know it is. I just read it. It is on page 248 of the bill. How does the hon. member think the Public Service unions are going to react to this?

Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member knows how the members of the Public Service unions will react to this. They will react to it with outrage. By reintroducing exactly what was defeated in the committee, the government not only did not take the committee process seriously, as the hon. member points out; it may have actually extended the reach of what was found offensive in committee.
This is a new twist on how not to pay attention to committees. The committee defeats something because it thinks it goes too far. The government agrees and says it will solve the problem; get it defeated in committee and then when it comes to the House, it will bring in something that goes even further.
Whatever the case may be, a horrible precedent has been set that will provide a real and unjust imbalance in the relationship between labour and management at Revenue Canada and any other place where this might apply. Madam Speaker, to continue along that same line of explanation for the bill presently going through the House of Commons, I draw the attention of members to page 248 of this bill.

Would the employer find out how much money the person does or does not have, whether or not he or she is

supporting children somewhere, what charities he or she gives to, or what political parties he or she contributed to? That is all information available under the privacy of a person's income tax return to the entire Public Service of Canada now. It would involve employees of employment and immigration who deal indirectly with the Unemployment Insurance Act in employment measures such as section 25, all employees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, all employees who deal directly or indirectly with the Canada Pension Plan, and all employees who deal directly or indirectly with Revenue Canada.
What is this? The Public Service Alliance of Canada must immediately act and demand a hearing because there is closure in this place. This bill will come to a vote in this place without having any hearings on that section of the act. It will come to a vote this evening so there is nothing the unions can do. There is nothing the employees can do. There is nothing members of Parliament can do. The only option, I suppose, under our system is to go to the Senate and ask it for hearings.
That is what we are passing in this bill. Just imagine when all the employees in the McCurdy conference in Gander, Newfoundland, are being looked at for promotions or salaries. They will have their income tax returns examined. That authorization is given under this bill. All the employees in Grand Falls, Newfoundland, working with employment and immigration can have their income tax returns sent to their bosses to evaluate. That is what is in the bill. That is what we are passing today in the House of Commons.
The member for Mississauga South stood in this Chamber the other day and gave the rationale for this change. Somebody in Revenue Canada appeared before the Federal Court relating to a case in which the person's income tax return was necessary but could not be obtained in advance of the charges being laid. This is why the change was being made in the law because this person could have been disciplined before the case came to the Federal Court.
That member stood and said it and another member stood and said it. Imagine. Because of a case before the Federal Court involving somebody at Revenue Canada, the bill is being changed to give the income tax return of everybody working for the federal government to their bosses for supervision and evaluation purposes. That is not the only change made in the bill.
