There is another change here that I just noticed. It did not receive any discussion in committee. It is for people who expect returns from Revenue Canada. Ordinary taxpayers have to pay interest from the time they file or April 30, whichever is later. The government has now changed three sections of the bill: clauses 77(1), 78(1) and so on. Interest will not be paid back now until 45 days after April 30 or after the date filed plus 45 days, whichever is later.
In the fairness package introduced by the Government of Canada last year in this Chamber, it said under fairness that Revenue Canada would pay interest back to the taxpayer just as the taxpayer had to pay interest to Revenue Canada. Now it has changed under this legislation.
This is most incredible, mind-boggling and baffling. We talk about lawyers. There were two members arguing a point a few moments ago. A legal opinion was given in this Chamber and it was given before the committee concerning the reason for the change in the trust law. All people had to do was to use the member's reasoning.
The member for Mississauga South says that all one has to do is to change the trustees. Imagine, all one has to do, he said, was to change the trustees to get around paying the tax. I hope the people in the auditing section of Revenue Canada were listening to members of Parliament when they stood in this Chamber and said that all one had to do was to change the trustees.
We have people employed in the Government of Canada. When one files a return on a trust, a T-3, and it comes up that the trustees are changed there is a little light that goes on in the computer. They want to know why. If it is found that those trustees were changed to avoid the taxes then somebody would be in trouble. GAAR, the General Anti-Avoidance Rule, would be after them. That is the law of this country.
There is a law in this country so that one cannot intentionally avoid paying taxes by simply changing the trustees in a trust. One cannot do it. If one can then a lot of people should be fired in Revenue Canada. I suppose there is something even more alarming than that nonsense that all one has to do to get around paying taxes is to just change a few trustees.
Apart from that, there is the incredible rationale used by the Government of Canada. Here we have the dean of law of the University of Victoria, the associate dean of law of Osgoode Hall and two tax experts, one in Toronto and one in Ottawa, claiming that this is a giveaway to some of the wealthiest people in Canada.
Members of Parliament did not say it. Some members of Parliament have said it over the years. One can read it sometimes in books that have been written to analyse our income tax system. Here we have the experts saying that this is a big giveaway. At the same time we have cut back our transfers to the provincial governments. We have not only cut back to the province of Newfoundland but we have demanded money back.
Imagine this. On the same day that one says one is going to forgive $145 million to two foreign banks that have nothing to do with trade with this nation, there is a bit of diplomacy.
One says to the Government of Newfoundland: "You have to pay back another $100 million because we believe you were overpaid". "Because the system has changed in counting people and we miscounted the population, you have to pay back money, province of Newfoundland, province of Saskatchewan, province of Nova Scotia and province of Prince Edward Island".
It brings in the GST and it taxes people and now it has the experts saying: "But it is giving the biggest tax break that we know of to the wealthiest people in Canada". How does one rationalize that? How does one rationalize putting off the payment of taxes that would have come due this year in 1993? How does one rationalize putting off the payment of those taxes while one puts the GST on ordinary people?
There is no rationale to any of this. There is no reasoning that the Government of Canada can come up with to do what it is doing here today.
A lot of new things happened to our income tax system in 1993. For the first time in 1993, for example, if somebody owes money to the Unemployment Insurance Commission they now have their rebate attached for the

first time in Canadian history. It was never done before. I represented a group of carpenters before a federal judge one day. These three carpenters had incorporated themselves-there were other people involved-into a company for what they called bidding purposes, to do bids on jobs. It was judged by national revenue that their unemployment insurance contributions were not for insurable employment because it was not, what is called under the act, at arm's length from the administration of the company.
We had to prove that the company was not formed for the purpose of collecting unemployment insurance. A judgment is given by the judge in this case. Therefore one is left with having to determine whether or not they formed the company just to collect unemployment insurance. One of the chaps was on the stand and the judge said: "Did you form the company so you could collect unemployment insurance?" The fellow says: "Yes, sir, of course that was one of the reasons. I would be a fool not to. What can one do in the middle of winter? Of course one is going to claim unemployment insurance". The judgment came down against those three carpenters. They have to pay back money now from about the last five years. There are endless numbers of these cases.
However, under the meaning of the Unemployment Insurance Act they committed fraud. They fraudulently obtained unemployment insurance. It was unknowing but it is fraud. They will not get a Revenue Canada return until all that money is paid back. It will just be seized now. All the arrangements that were made for pay back are all cancelled. All their returns from Revenue Canada will be seized. Not a week goes by that it does not happen. The unemployment insurance offices throughout this country supply a list of names to Revenue Canada in that province and the action is taken. That is every week.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member says: "Hear, hear". There is a real Tory talking: "Hear, hear". Sock it to the poor guys. The rich get richer, the poor get poorer and the middle class get the shaft. That is Tory philosophy and that is what has happened under this bill.
Just imagine our country in the state it is in financially and with the debt up. Just examine the debt. As the Liberal critic, the hon. member for Sudbury, said in this House a few moments ago, the Prime Minister in his resignation speech said: "I have left the Tory party in an extremely good financial position". I congratulate the hon. member for Gander-Grand Falls for his excellent speech. He underlined the fact that this bill is meant for the wealthy, for the very rich, to allow them to accumulate even more money, to grant them even more tax exemptions, while hitting the other people, the less well off and the medium income citizens.
We have only a few hours, not several days, to consider this bill. I find it surprising, even scandalous, that the government through this legislation will be able to assess the performance of its employees, in some areas, by looking at what used to be secret and sacred, namely their tax returns.
When Canadians fill out their income tax returns, they do it in all honesty, confident that the federal government will never use the information for performance assessment purposes such as promotion, demotion and even dismissal. This is surprising, but it is also shameful.
It is often said, in-

-Public Service 2000 that managers should manage a great bible of public service of the present government. Let managers manage.

Madam Speaker, I will read the exact section: "use or provide to any person taxpayer information solely for the purpose relating to the supervision, evaluation or discipline of an authorized person who assists" in any way, shape or form "administration or enforcement of this act" which is the Income Tax Act,
the Canada Pension Plan or the Unemployment Insurance Act. That is exactly what it is.
Yet when these employees fill out their income tax returns it will not be confidential. Of course I have this little old special tax guide. Oh how uncomplicated my financial affairs must be. This little guide, even a reduced form, shows a declaration of taxpayers' rights, privacy and confidentiality. It covers every taxpayer, but that goes right clean out through the window in these circumstances.
In relation to the hon. member's first observation, he is right because back in 1971 we had an inheritance tax. The Liberals cancelled it, threw it out.
It was replaced by the capital gains tax which at that time was half the normal rate of taxation. It was replaced. The members who were bringing it in, the Minister of Finance at the time upon advice of the finance department and the revenue department said: "Look, what about people who might not pay what was the inheritance tax prior to 1971, replaced by the capital gains in 1972 upon death, because their assets are in trust?"
The 21-year rule was passed. Some people call it an arbitrary figure but I do not think any figure is more arbitrary than death under this bill. The law was that every 21 years it would have to be paid. The money that would normally have been paid, that every small businessman pays, that every normal person pays, would have to paid in 21 years. Twenty-one years from 1972 is 1993, this year. Lo and behold, the government brings in a bill now to cancel the 21-year rule and to let it go for another 40 or 50 years.
Those are the undeniable, indisputable facts behind this legislation that not one member on the government side can deny. Nobody in Canada can deny that and that is why it is such an outrage.

Madam Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate to try to refute some of the nonsense that I have been listening to from the other side. There are two particular points I would immediately like to address, one from the speaker who just sat down commenting about how our Prime Minister has left our party in great shape.

I guess I would only compare it to the prime ministers who preceded our Prime Minister, who not only left our country in absolutely terrible shape but left the Liberal Party virtually bankrupt. Not only did the Liberals wreck the country financially with their profligate spending methods, after they lost the election federally they transferred all those people who used to work for the Liberal government in the early eighties to Ontario where David Peterson gladly said: "Join us; we would love to have you". They then proceeded to increase spending in the province of Ontario at a rate of about 15 per cent a year and did exactly to the province of Ontario what they had done to the whole country. But so much for the Liberal record of the past.
I find it somewhat disturbing that an opposition member would stand and say that because there was a quorum call; we are using up debating time. They are the ones who called these things. I can assure everybody there are lots of Conservatives listening to what they have to say. However, they choose not to speak; they would just as soon choose to count.
I would like to get to the subject matter of Bill C-92 because I am sure that is what members would like me to comment on. There are a number of factors in Bill C-92. The first I would like to deal with is this issue of the $100,000 capital gains exemption.
I understand the concern that exists with removing the $100,000 exemption on passive investments. Passive investments such as real estate are probably the most well-known example. An individual may decide to purchase a second house or a third house and because of inflation it increases in value after a given period of time, whether it is two months or two years, sell it and take the capital gain.
Under the old system they could generally have a capital gain of up to $100,000 and not have to pay tax on it. Under this system they are going to have to pay tax on that income. Some will argue, what about those people who take that second property and use it as a rental property, possibly help provide low cost housing or rental housing in a market that desperately needs it? Yes, those people are looking for capital gains to accrue on that particular property.
Government Orders
What usually happens on those properties is that the person who owns the property is depreciating it through wise accounting methods to increase, if there is any profit in the rental business, that profit by taking capital losses or by depreciating the property value.
They are in fact trying to avoid paying taxes legally. It is not an illegal thing to do, and is very appropriate for those who wish to invest. They can still do it and have their capital gain on the property if they set themselves up in a small business with shares. The shareholdings of that company will increase in value. That becomes an active investment rather than a passive investment.
They have injected some capital into a small business. They have gone into the rental business and at the end of whatever period of time they think is appropriate to take their capital gain, they can take it. It is not just on $100,000, but since they have set it up as a business and the business has some equity and assets, they could potentially go up to $500,000 in capital gain because they are going to be actively investing and promoting a business.
That is what this legislation is designed to do. It is designed to reward people who invest actively in the creation of wealth within Canada; the creation of wealth through the creation of rental properties, if that should be the decision of the investor; or the injection of capital into a small manufacturing company or a small service company. At the end of the period of time it can be sold and they can have up to a $500,000 capital gain.
We on this side of the House are saying, if they are going to have a capital gain it is because they have actively invested in an enterprise that is creating wealth and economic activity rather than a passive investment which is simply sitting on a house and because it has gone up in value through inflation, they have a capital gain.
Certainly in my riding, back in 1988 and 1989, in fact in most of the greater Toronto region and in fact probably in a lot of Canada, people were being, shall we say, junior Reichmanns. The idea was to buy a property because it was going to go up in value. They would then buy a second and a third property, not because they had invested anything in increasing the value of that property. They simply wanted to take a capital gain because of inflation.

April 1, 1993
Government Orders
We know what has happened to the Reichmanns. It is fair to say that a lot of that has happened to the small Reichmanns. It does not make me happy to see people losing money they have invested, but in this world when they invest money they have an opportunity to make a gain. Similarly because of our system of free enterprise there is also an equal opportunity to lose. People will just have to be very cautious about how that works.
Another portion of this bill deals with trusts. The trust rules were established back in 1972 to deal with the change in the tax structure, as was mentioned by members of the opposition. We were going to replace an estate tax with a capital gains tax. There was a transition period where trusts had been established and there had to be some mechanism to deal with those trusts.
We have heard a lot of comments about witnesses who appeared before the committee. Certainly they are very knowledgeable people, I do not question that at all, and very talented in their particular fields. But as always happens, as I have found, Madam Speaker, and I am sure you have found in your experience here in the House, on any given subject we can have a whole series of expert witnesses each saying something totally opposite to what the other expert has said. It is our role as members of Parliament to listen to all the expertise that is available to us and arrive at a decision, a conclusion.
Some members of the opposition have listened to Professor Neil Brooks, who I might add is very closely tied to Bob Rae and his friends in Toronto, who have accepted the advice of Bob Rae. We know what Bob Rae is doing to the province of Ontario. We know that he is a profligate spender. We know how he loves to tax. We will accept that Neil Brooks in his reflections to the committee had a point, very knowledgeable in his own right, but not a point that I would necessarily agree with.
I think we will find as we look at all these committee reports that we each have to make judgment calls. I am not suggesting that the NDP judgment on Professor Neil Brooks is right or wrong. Suffice to say it is different than my judgment on what he had to say and I prefer my judgment over theirs in this particular instance.
What we have is a problem of this perception being created that trusts are created for the wealthy only and that there is some huge pile of money, billions and billions, sitting there untaxed.
First off, trusts are not created by the wealthy only. They are created for almost anybody who would like to take advantage of them. Let me give some examples because undoubtedly we can reference some large, wealthy families who would establish trusts. However we do not really know who has all these trusts.
There can be circumstances where a family owns a family cottage. The parents have four children and would like to make sure that this cottage stays in the family for all the family to use in the future. They establish a trust so that the family does not get into a squabble over which of the four kids owns the cottage. Do they each have 25 per cent? What happens when the bills come in? Who pays? All those things can happen. It is possible for couples to establish a trust to oversee the management of assets such as a cottage. In order to establish that trust they have to pay capital gains tax on the cottage.
Today we are going to take this cottage from the private ownership of this couple and put it into a trust. They have to value the cottage and to pay capital gains on the cottage. We have eliminated the $100,000 capital gains so we will assume that this is a second home for the people. They have to pay the capital gains on the increased value of the cottage as they put it into the trust. It was not free of tax going in.
For argument's sake the cottage is rented out all year round and it generates revenue to the trust. That revenue minus the expenses-we will assume that there is a profit at the end of the year-each and every year is taxed so that any profit accruing to the trust has income tax paid on it.
That trust under these rules can run until the death of the last of the four children. At that point if the trust or the children who are in a sense the beneficiaries of the trust have decided they are going to leave the cottage to their children, the trust should at the death of the last of the original four children value the cottage, declare the capital gains that have accrued from the day the cottage went into the trust to the day the cottage went out of the trust because of the death of the last child, pay the capital gains and a new trust is therefore created for the next generation.
April 1, 1993

All the way through there is avoidance or delay of tax. In fact one might argue that this couple who put the cottage in trust 40 years before they died and declared capital gains at year one lent the Government of Canada the tax they paid at that point interest free for 40 years because they would not have had to pay it until they died.
I realize that is an argument that is not being made by others on the other side, but the fact of the matter is that the trust is paying, up front, the capital gains accrued which it would not have to pay under normal circumstances until the death of both parents.
I have used the cottage as a very simple example. It could be a small business where there is an entrepreneur with a local hardware store, a grocery store or a comer store. The entrepreneur could be leaving the business to his or her children. The same rules apply. This idea that it is for the rich is nonsense.
Yes, they can take advantage of these rules just as well as anyone else can. Yes, they may have a greater interest in doing so. The fact of the matter is that these rules are not just created for them.
There is this perception that there are these huge sums of money out there. The fact is that simply because one owns an asset does not mean one has to pay capital gains on it. One only has to pay capital gains when one sells the asset. They would lead one to believe on the other side that one has these trusts sitting with $6 billion, $8 billion, $10 billion or $12 billion worth of assets tax free.
There is no tax owing on them. It is no different for you or I. What is our asset value? For argument's sake we would possibly own a house. We may have some minor investments. It does not matter what they are worth. There is no tax owing on them. It is the same with a trust. Simply because the trust has $100,000 in assets or $1 million in assets or $100 million in assets does not mean there is any tax owing on that money.
The only time a trust owes tax is when the trust generates income. They pay income tax at one of the highest going rates in Canada. A trust is not some way of sheltering income because the trust pays income tax invariably at a rate higher than an individual would pay. All the way through for 5, 10 or 15 years, every year, the trust must file a tax return and pay the tax owing on the income it has generated that year. Of course at the end of the time, if the trust is closed down, if it is transferred
Government Orders
to other beneficiaries because of the death of the last beneficiary of the trust, a capital gains tax must be paid on the increase in value of the assets. This idea that trusts sit there tax free outside the rules is really not correct.
There is concern raised about the 21-year rule as it was created in 1972. Now we have come to 1993 and 21 years is up, and these trusts that were a function of 1972 all of a sudden owe a fortune in taxes.
First, they may owe a fortune in tax if there was any capital gains. There is no knowledge of whether there was or was not. There have been an awful lot of companies in this country with assets that have shrunk tremendously over the last 21 years and are technically bankrupt. There is no argument that says they owe a nickel. They may. That is true.
What is not mentioned is that under the rules created in 1972 if a trust ran the entire 21 years it would have to pay the tax. However, it is possible after 18 years or 19 years for the trust to owe a lot of tax in two years' time so it creates a new trust with a new trustee. All the assets from the old trust will be transferred to the new trust. No tax would be owed on that transfer. Lo and behold, what do they have? They have another 21 years to go.
The idea that tax was owed after 21 years is absolute nonsense because it was possible based on the 1972 rules to simply transfer from trust to trust to trust ad infinitum. In 500 years from now one could have these trusts still going and never paying capital gains.
That is why I am surprised that the opposition would be opposed to what we are doing. We are saying no longer can one go ad infinitum transferring from one trust to the next trust to the next trust. We are saying there is a beneficiary recognized in the trust. When that last beneficiary dies, which can only be immediate members of the family, the trust has to declare and pay its capital gains even though the trust may in fact be putting the money into another trust for the grandchildren or great-grandchildren. The fact is that every time there is a transfer of the trust from generation to generation there must be a payment of capital gains, whereas under the existing rules of 1972 there never needs to be a payment of capital gains because the trust can go on ad infinitum for as long as it wishes.

April 1, 1993
Government Orders
One can see I do not have any problems supporting this particular requirement because we are bringing into force some regulations on trusts and their ability to avoid paying taxes.
If assets are put into a trust, which is obviously what has excited most members of the opposition, then capital gains are paid going into it, as I mentioned. Income tax is paid on the increased valuation based on income earned rather than on inflationary valuation. Income tax is paid as the years go by. Let us presume that a trust, instead of going for 21 years or going to the next generation, simply goes for five years. At that point they decide they are going to take something out of the trust to give to the beneficiaries and pass the value to the people, usually children, who are looking for some cash so they can meet mortgage payments or whatever.
Under the rules the trust would have to value the assets, pay capital gains at that point and then make its payment to the beneficiaries.
From my perspective on the trusts there is every control to make sure that taxes are paid all the time all the way through the system. In fact we closed what I think was a major loophole in allowing the trust to continue to be rolled from one trust to the other.
I just want to make sure I have covered all the major points in my presentation. I see that I have hit everything I wanted to raise. I only have one minute left anyway. I will sit down and that will give the opposition another minute to ask a question or two.

Madam Speaker, we on this side of the House are concerned about the protection of estates in trust. We are very concerned about that both from the point of view of the taxpayer and fairness in the taxation system. I will be speaking shortly on subclause 137(1) and specifically subparagraph (h) of that clause on page 247.
The member who has just spoken on behalf of the government will be well aware that this clause was not reported from committee. It was removed from the bill. It has now been reintroduced and even expanded by the government at this stage.
I was quite surprised since this clause deals with the right to have private taxpayer information for the purpose of the supervision, evaluation or discipline of an
employee of the Government of Canada not only in the department dealing with taxation but in two other departments.
The President of the Treasury Board, who is nominally the employer of these employees to be supervised, evaluated or disciplined, knows nothing about this clause. That is understandable because this is a bill arising from another minister.
I wonder if the member who has just spoken on behalf of the government could explain why this clause is here and why the government wants to be able to dig into people's personal tax forms for supervising, evaluating or disciplining employees of the Government of Canada.
It already has very strict guidelines, regulations or even legislation as to how supervision, evaluation or discipline is to be carried out. It has just expanded the discretion that the employer has with respect to discipline. I am at a loss. No member of the government has yet explained why the government feels it needs this excessive power.

Madam Speaker, it is evident as I made comments in my opening remarks about how experts appear before committee. Individuals make an interpretation of what they have to say.
The fact of the matter is that the government has very clearly said that it does not need to go through each and every income tax return of Canadians in establishing a case for or against a Revenue Canada employee.
Again I believe it is simply a matter of interpretation as to what is being mentioned. I understand the interest of the member. She certainly campaigned very hard to make sure that the Public Service of Canada had all the rights and that the Government of Canada had no rights. That has certainly been my observation of her interventions on behalf of her constituents.
I guess I would just say that somewhere there has to be a balance. This piece of legislation creates a balance that gives the Government of Canada and the people who work in Revenue Canada an opportunity to make sure that they have access, without going through the personal income tax return, to decide whether an employee in Revenue Canada should be disciplined or not based on work habits or whatever other reasons may be appropriate in the fulfilment of his or her employment with the Government of Canada.
April 1, 1993

Madam Speaker, I would like to comment on the reply just given by the hon. member for Ontario who obviously is not aware that I am the critic for the Public Service.
A small number of public servants live in my riding. Some 70 per cent of the 250,000 public servants in fact do not even live in the region of the national capital. He might want to be aware of that. I commented from the perspective of public policy with respect to the Public Service and not from parochial concern for my own constituents, which I carry into everything I do in this House.
I am afraid we have not had a terribly good explanation, considering this is really an exception to our normal rule of privacy about people's income tax returns. The member for Ontario might want to try to explain again why the government feels it needs this authority. It has substantial authority, which he seems not to be aware of, under the Financial Administration Act, the Public Service Employment Act, policies of the departments and codes of conduct of the departments, to discipline, supervise and evaluate. It has almost total discretion to do precisely that, far more than in the private sector.
In light of that I would like to give the member another opportunity to explain why the government feels it needs this authority. Clearly this makes it possible for the government to release personal income tax forms to other persons, such as somebody's supervisor, director or chief, for any purpose relating to supervision. Tb me that means any supervisor can ask to see the income tax form of a certain employee for any reason and it may be released to him or her.
I would really like the hon. member to try to clarify why it is there. It was removed at committee so why did the government seek not only to reintroduce it but expand it to include anybody working on the Canada Pension Plan directly or indirectly and anybody having anything to do with the Unemployment Insurance Act?

Madam Speaker, I would first like to state I was not being negative about the efforts the member makes on behalf of her own constituents. I would hope we all take similar approaches to representing our constituents, but sometimes there is a fine line between
Government Orders
the interests of our constituents and the interests of Canada as a whole.
The member for Mississauga South spoke extensively at report stage on the particular question she is raising. I guess I would encourage her to read the comments of the member for Mississauga South, which I think will quite adequately reflect and answer the concerns she has raised.
I would also ask the member to refer to the representations of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, Mr. Bruce Phillips, who also issued both letters and comments to the committee on the matter she is raising. As the privacy commissioner Mr. Phillips is certainly not raising any major concerns as he sees it with regard to the bill, the particular clauses and reference.

Madam Speaker, there are a couple of principal points I want to raise before I discuss the measures, some of which have been the subject of discussion this afternoon and some of which have not.
There are a number of things that bother me about this bill. First, we are now going back to measures that were passed on February 25, 1992. It is now April 1,1993. Notwithstanding the closure we have discussed in this House and the slowness of doing business, and totally irrespective of the closure procedures this government continues to invoke, this is an unconscionable time to actually implement tax measures given the difficulty we have with our well-known public deficit and our federal and total national debt.
I want to put into perspective the background of my concern over the length of time it has taken and some of the measures that are contained in this bill as a result of the first 1992 budget if we discount the December budget.
We are now in a position where our national debt has become an instrument and an issue of great concern to all Canadians. It is very difficult to pick up a newspaper or a magazine or listen to any radio station, AM or FM, country and western or serious classical music, without a mention being made of the national debt of Canada within a relatively short time. Although it gives me no comfort that the national debt of most of the G-7 countries is a concern, I take no comfort in knowing we

Government Orders
are second only to Italy with regard to this sad situation we are in.
As I have said in this House more than once, and I need to repeat it again as a backdrop to the presentation I have today, it is not just the amount of the national debt or the federal debt, and I differentiate between them. The federal debt is what the federal government owes and the national debt is what the federal government plus the provincial governments owe. To use a figure alone, although it might be startling, may not be the true measure of what it is we actually owe. Let me amplify that.
In 1984, which I am going to use as a benchmark when this government came to power, the federal debt of the country was $168 billion. I have heard $170 billion used for round figures, but I think, Mr. Speaker, you will find $168 billion is the correct figure.
In a speech given by the finance minister of the day when the government took over shortly after Labour Day in 1984, the deficit was in the vicinity of $35 billion. Through rearrangement of the figures and creative accounting within a short time the deficit went up to about $38 billion. In round figures the deficit in 1984 was around $35 billion. Whether it was $38 billion or $33 billion, through bookkeeping it was in the vicinity of $35 billion.
In four years not much has changed. In almost nine years we are left with essentially the same deficit of $34.5 billion projected on December 3. The finance minister is only too quick to point out they are 1993 dollars and are a lot less than they were in 1984.1 will grant him that. That is a fair statement to make.
What the finance minister does not say is that the national debt has doubled. It was $168 billion and two weeks ago a clock in Vancouver showed the doomsday national debt at $450 billion, which is much more than double, and it is going up at the rate of over $1,000 a second.
The true measure of our debt is how much we owe compared to how much we make. In 1984 when we had a debt of $168 billion we owed 42 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product. In other words we owed less than 50
per cent of what we made. That is pretty high. If I owed 50 per cent of what I made I would be a little bit worried. If a business owed 50 per cent of what it made, generally speaking it would be worried about its cash flow and its future.
Almost nine years later where do we stand? We stand in a much worse condition because right now we are approaching a ratio of debt to Gross Domestic Product of 70 per cent. The closest figure I can come up with is 68 per cent. That means we are more than 50 per cent worse off than we were eight and a half years ago.
I do not care how one cooks the books. I do not care how one presents the figures. I do not care how one measures trade deficit imbalances and consumer spending. That is considered by most economists and most people in the business to be an accurate assessment of the financial ability of a country to continue.
Clearly the finance minister is worried about this and the government is worried about this. If one reads through his statements, and I believe he has as much as come out and said it, one will find that the December 3 mini budget, the financial statement of the government, was to calm and assuage the concerns of the foreign countries to which we are in debt.
This is much more of a problem than it was nine years ago, because nine years ago less than 10 per cent of that 42 per cent of our GDP that we owed was owed to foreigners. Today it is now 30 per cent and growing.
I would suspect that when the Minister of Finance comes forth in April, May, or June, whenever it is he is going to present his budget, we are going to be looking at not sorting out the problems of the country but once more assuaging and comforting those foreign interests that are watching us very closely with respect to our credit rating and our ability to borrow money as we continue to get ourselves more deeply mired in the situation.
It is my regrettable belief that we are living in a world of advanced disillusion. I used to think that with every budget the government would be able to sort this mess out.
April 1, 1993

I am now convinced that it has lost control. It has taxed as much as it can. There is no room for taxation. We have the goods and services tax. Services are being taxed. We have borrowed as much as we can borrow. Now we are in a position where all that is left for the government to do is to blame it on the Liberals nine years ago and to implement, I was going to use the expression nickel and dime but that is not a very sophisticated expression, measures like those measures being implemented in Bill C-92. It will barely scratch the surface of what we really need to get this country back in shape financially.
Let me speak to this bill. It went through first reading on November 26, 1992. It had second reading in February, started report stage on March 29 and resumed it on March 30, the day before yesterday, and it is now going through third reading.
There is another aspect of this bill that bothers me. I have found myself as a legislator, a member of Parliament and a parliamentarian caught in the dilemma of looking at bills put forward by the government. This one is over one inch thick. I would say it is about one and a quarter inches thick. I have been through it. It is very difficult to go through it in detail with the time one has, but I have zeroed in and focused on those parts of the bill with which I am concerned.
There are some very good measures in this bill, such as the reinstitution of the small business development bond program, and reduction of the manufacturing and corporate income tax rates which may be debatable. There is also the introduction of the homeowners plan which allows individuals to use up to $20,000 of their RRSP funds to purchase a home before March 2 of this year, a reduction of the individual surtax from 5 per cent to 3 per cent, and a measure to assist Canadians with disabilities. There are other measures of which I am very much in favour. They have been a long time in coming and I am very much in support of them.
However there are other aspects that have been discussed in this House, and I am not going to go through them all. The one thing that I find to be very inconsistent with the reported quest of the government to find every penny it can to retire the debt of the country is that it would implement such a measure concerning private trusts.
My hon. colleague from Sudbury has done considerable and excellent work in committee, in the House and
Government Orders
in her role as a critic in bringing to the attention of the Canadian public the difficulties that we have with a clause in the bill that refers to the 21-year rule of private trusts.
If one reads what is in the bill, starting in clause 42, it would be very difficult for the average person to really understand what it was that was taking place here. Essentially what clause 42 does is continue the extension of the 21-year exemption. In effect this clause really opens a loophole to those Canadians who are in the highest income bracket and those who can afford to have million dollar trust funds set aside.
It opens a loophole which really allows them not to pay taxes until a time in the future, anywhere from 20 to 40 years from now. We do not know how long because it depends on the demise of the last member of a family who would be the recipient of the trust fund. It could be 80 years. Eighty years from now my grandchildren and perhaps my great-grandchildren, and the grandchildren and great-grandchildren of members of the House of Commons, will be looking at different problems.
Our problem with the national debt is a problem of today. The government introduced the GST at the most inopportune and difficult time, when more than 90 per cent of Canadians disagreed with the principle of the goods and services tax and with its implementation at a time when the country was about to go into a recession that was made by our own government, by its own admission.
I am told by the experts that in order to collect a dollar through the goods and services tax when the tax was implemented it cost the government 51 cents. In other words for every dollar that was paid by a consumer on goods and services only 49 cents went to retiring the debt.
Then I juxtapose that against the manufacturers' sales tax which it was supposed to replace, and which was not a tax on services. Maybe 20,000 businesses were subjected to the tax at 13 per cent, which was raised from 8 per cent over the years as part of the 38 tax increases that this government has imposed on Canadians. It took in $17.5 billion, $2 billion more than the net impact of the goods and services tax. More important, with that tax it cost only five cents to collect a dollar.

April 1, 1993
Government Orders
By anybody's imagination that manufacturers' sales tax, irrespective of its pros and cons, advantages and disadvantages, from an administrative and an efficiency perspective was 10 times more efficient than the goods and services tax. It was certainly a lot more popular too.
I am told by organizations in the business that the goods and services tax will cost businesses $3 billion to collect and around $5 billion to be compliant with. We are looking at $10 billion that businesses had to spend in order to implement this tax.
I cannot understand the inconsistency of allowing loopholes that will allow hundreds of millions of dollars, even billions of dollars, to escape the tax collector. I do not know what the figure is; nobody knows what the figures are. How do we know how much a trust is going to be in future years?
One of the figures that I have heard mentioned in a newspaper article is $10 billion. This would be an open loophole that would allow $10 billion to slide through the taxman's fingers at a time when we are looking for every cent from the lower class, the middle class and people without jobs. They have to pay GST on the very food they buy, that is taxable, and the services they receive, from a haircut to a mechanic working on their car to do required maintenance so they can provide transportation for a family. That is very unfair.
I heard three or four hon. members from the other side defend this tax, and I would expect them to defend it because it is part of the government's bill. I would say that I would not like to be in the position, at least in the constituency that I represent, of having to get on my feet and defend the passage of billions of dollars not being collected from those who could most afford it compared to those who can least afford it, those who have to pay over 90 per cent of their disposable income to the taxman in goods and services. It is grossly unfair and it is a measure of which the government cannot be proud.
While the Prime Minister may boast that his party coffers are in good shape financially, I do not expect that many members of the few who are running again on the other side of the House will be using this as an election issue. It is something of which I do not believe even those who speak in favour of it are proud.
There is another aspect of this bill that I find inconsistent. It is inconsistent with any government that supports its employees. I refer to the roughly 20,000 public servants who are employed in Revenue Canada.
I happen to have a great deal of respect for the Public Service of Canada. I think we have one of the finest public services in the world. I have had experience with many. I have worked with public servants and we should be proud of the work they do. They are not just in Ottawa; they are all throughout Canada. In my riding they operate federal offices from fisheries inspection offices to unemployment insurance centres. While we do not always agree on the way things should be done, I have found that in their application and their professionalism they are as good as there is. Their reputation will stand up against any in any country.
There is a lot of stress involved in working in the Public Service. Public servants are under a lot of pressure to produce. I would like to digress for a second with regard to the cod moratorium. While I do not always agree with the officials of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans I have nothing but the greatest respect for the way they have applied themselves in their jobs in an attempt to provide a service to people. Their package is not always acceptable to constituents who do not qualify, but nonetheless one has to have the highest regard for the amount of work they do in trying to deliver the service they have been asked to deliver by our government.
The clause to which my hon. colleague from Ottawa West made reference is inconsistent with fair treatment of government employees. I have been in this House for a relatively short time and I have been unhappy about some of the comments that have been made and some of the measures that have been taken. I do not want to open old wounds, but I cannot let this go without comment.
I want to make a point about clause 137, which was not initially there but was actually introduced. It takes away the privacy of these 20,000 public servants who are under pressure as it is and allows the system to look at their income tax returns in situations of supervision, discipline or something of that nature.
April 1, 1993

Those two aspects, the loophole for the rich and the business of lack of privacy for individuals in the revenue department, should be disallowed. It is because of those two negative aspects, despite the good things in this bill, that I will not be able to find it possible to vote for the bill.
