Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago the Department of the Environment announced that it would terminate the contract this fall that has provided a manned weather station at the Gore Bay-Manitoulin airport and automate the system. This decision would cost the community six jobs in a district in which unemployment is already too high.
However the implications of this action go far beyond the provision of weather information and unemployment. An automated system will not provide the information on air traffic, airport runway conditions or personalized weather information to pilots and mariners in the north channel area and could jeopardize public safety.
Likewise, because the Department of Transport does not provide services at this airport, the weather station personnel have provided the refuelling of aircraft, parking, landing fees collection, and customs and tourist
information at the airport. If these services were removed the airport's viability would be drastically downgraded to the point where the regularly scheduled NorOntair services could be put in jeopardy.
We intend to fight this wrong-headed decision with every means at our disposal. I call on the Minister of the Environment to reverse this decision and renew the contract for a manned weather station at the Gore Bay-Manitoulin airport.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I would like to mention that the Government of Canada, by participating in the program to buy back commercial fishing licences for Atlantic salmon on the North Shore, is contributing directly to perpetuating this species and also contributing to the development of sport fishing in Quebec.
With the program, of which 70 per cent is funded by our government, more than 60 commercial licences in the riding of Manicouagan will be bought back. This will help the Atlantic salmon stocks recover in all the rivers between Franklin and La Romaine on the North Shore of the St. Lawrence. It will also emphasize the development of sport fishing, which helps stabilize the economy of isolated communities on the North Shore.
The program will treat commercial fishermen fairly by giving them reasonable compensation for their gear and for the loss of income that they will incur. This participation is made possible by the Federal Office of Regional Development in Quebec.
This is something concrete that our government is doing for sustainable development and the survival of the Atlantic salmon.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians were astonished to learn Monday that the government has now determined that the internment during World War I of more than 5,000 utterly blameless persons of Ukrainian origin was "not of national historic significance".

April 1, 1993
Therefore there will be no interpretive centre near the largest internment camp at Castle Mountain in Banff National Park and no markers at the other 25 camps, this despite the fact that it was the Ukrainian internees whose forced labour built much of Banff park.
By unanimous resolution this very House deemed the internments to be unwarranted and unjust and called on the government to mark the 26 camp sites and establish "a permanent historic educational exhibit" at Castle Mountain.
The entire NDP caucus stands by that motion. We call on the government to reverse the decision made public this week, build the interpretive centre, mark the other internment sites, formally apologize to the Ukrainian community, and speedily settle the other outstanding redress questions.

Mr. Speaker, the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board gained tough new power under Bill C-91 that will allow it to review the prices of new patented medicines.
All medicines are not patented. In fact most drugs in drug stores are not patented. When the patent on a drug expires it can be produced by anyone. The Patented Medicine Prices Review Board does not have any power over drug prices once the patent has expired.
I would like to point out that some time ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare asked his officials to work with their provincial counterparts to develop a Canadian agency for pharmaceutical information assessment so that Canadian consumers would have the necessary information to compare the prices of non-patented medicines, ensuring that they could get the correct drug at the best possible price.

Mr. Speaker, on March 18, 1993 the Dogrib people signed a
$125 million agreement with the Northwest Territories Power Corporation for the development of hydroelectric power in the Dogrib-North Slave region of the Northwest Territories.
This historical agreement is a commercial undertaking that will balance the interests of both parties and will address the legitimate concerns and sensitivities of the traditional economy of the Dogrib with today's opportunities for development in the region.
This brave and bold move by the Dogrib has set an example for all Dene. In developing environmentally sound partnerships with industry they are providing economic security and meaningful job training for their people. It also gives them tremendous strength at the negotiating table for land claims.
I would like to wish the Dogrib nation a very happy and prosperous future. In doing so I congratulate Grand Chief Joe Rabesca of Rae, Chief Isadore Zoe of Lac La Martre, Chief Heniy Gon of Rae Lakes, and Chief Joseph Judas of Snare Lake.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my strong support for the recent agreement by the governments in Canada to reduce internal trade barriers.
The principle that governments will now treat people, goods, services and capital equally, irrespective of where they originate in Canada, is indeed positive news for our small businesses in Canada.
The growth, development and encouragement of our entrepreneurs and small businesses have been seriously hindered by these unnecessary limitations to free movement.
An efficient, open and integrated market in Canada is a must. It will improve the competitiveness of our small businesses in the domestic market and in export markets as more and more of them look outward.
The recent agreement to reduce interprovincial trade barriers is a major step forward for Canadian small business.
April 1, 1993

Mr. Speaker, during the intense debate on the North American free trade agreement that would bind us to Mexico, a low wage partner, and threaten thousands of jobs here in Canada intensity was shown on all sides of the House.
The government was in favour of the legislation. The Liberals allegedly were opposed, and so were the New Democrats and some of the Independents. The crunch came after time allocation, which in effect was closure.
The moment came for the vote to be taken. The government stood up and supported its policy. The combined opposition was prepared to stand and defeat the government. When the vote took place we found that there were 113 members for it and 94 against. Half the Liberal caucus did not show up for the vote.
Everybody in this country who is opposed to NAFTA should recognize that the Liberals did not show up in the House. They could have beaten the bill. Only six members paired. They could have defeated the bill when they had the chance but they did not show up. Why? You figure it out, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with enthusiasm and pride that I welcome the announcement of the renewal of the federal government strategy concerning the elderly that was made today by the Minister of State for Seniors.
Since 1988, when the first strategy was put in place, the quality of life of senior Canadians has been constantly improving. Indeed, many seniors from all over the country have, at one time or another, enjoyed the New Horizons Program or the Seniors Independence Program, for example.
The main objective of the renewed strategy is to build on the solid foundations of the first strategy in order to allow senior Canadians to take the place that they deserve in society.
The new elements of the renewed strategy, the Ventures for Independence Program and the development of
a federal policy on aging, should largely contribute to meet that objective.
At a time when departments are asked to reduce their programs, the commitment and the investment that have just been announced are a clear evidence of the long-term vision of the government and its firm commitment to enhance the independence and the quality of life of seniors in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in the government's mini budget last December the Minister of Finance announced that there would be an indefinite freeze on increases in grants in lieu of taxes to municipalities.
Residents of the city of Scarborough object to the federal government downloading its tax burden on to local property and business taxpayers. The federal government benefits from municipal services as do all property and business taxpayers.
This unilateral decision not to pay any increase in municipal taxes has the effect of off-loading those costs on to the weakest of our government structures and into a tax structure that is the least flexible and the most regressive.
I call upon the Minister of Finance to reverse his decision to freeze these grants and pick up the federal government's fair share of the local tax burden on Scarborough's constituents.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Seniors has announced today that the federal government will extend the Seniors Strategy for another five years.
This announcement shows our government's concern for the senior citizens of Canada. It is also an excellent way of helping our society prepare itself to meet the special needs of an aging population.

April 1, 1993
We are also introducing a new program called "Ventures for Independence". This program will give priority to innovative suggestions aimed at improving the quality of life and independence of seniors.
The development of a federal policy on aging is another new and important element of this strategy. By the year 2031, one in five Canadians will be over 65, and if we want today's and tomorrow's seniors to enjoy independence and dignity in their retirement, we can only be delighted about the renewal of the Seniors Strategy.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians should know that Bill C-91, legislation implementing the drug patent legislation, was passed back on December 10, 1992, thanks to the 21 NDP members who failed to show up for that crucial vote.
If the NDP had actually opposed giving multinational drug firms carte blanche with brand name drugs sold in Canada for the next 20 years, as it alleged, it would have demanded that every living, breathing member of its caucus show up. Instead, only half of the NDP caucus arrived for that final vote on what was described as the largest single affront to Canada's universal health care system since it was created.
Even the former B.C. premier, the member forEsqui-malt-Juan de Fuca, who opposed that Draconian drug patent legislation, did not show up in this House.
As a result of the fact that the NDP did not demand full attendance of its caucus for that crucial vote Canadians are facing higher costs for patent drugs in Canada. By failing to demonstrate its resolve the NDP has helped the Conservative government to allow-
The hon. member's time has expired. I know that other members in the House will breathe a sigh of great relief.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning, CBC quoted a spokesperson for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as saying that only 5 per cent of proceeds from cigarette smuggling are seized. It was also reported that, without a stricter law, the RCMP cannot deal with the problem.
I would like to point out that Bill C-102, which is now at report stage in the House, is designed to provide our police forces with the tools they need in their fight against tobacco smuggling.
I want to remind the House that the government is open to discussions with the provinces in order to address the issue of smuggling.

Mr. Speaker, the recommendations made yesterday by the Quebec Conseil de la langue franqaise for the replacement of Bill 178 are not acceptable.
This Draconian law, which bans English on commercial signs in Quebec, will automatically expire this year because it was passed in 1988 by using the notwithstanding clause to override the charter of rights, the Supreme Court, the Quebec Court of Appeal and the Quebec Superior Court.
Considering the importance of this matter, not only for Quebec but for minority language rights throughout Canada, I ask the Prime Minister and all members of Parliament to approach the Quebec government and urge it to opt for a replacement law which fully respects the 1988 Supreme Court decision and does not require the notwithstanding clause.
Such a solution should also respect the principle set out in the Charlottetown accord that Canadians and their governments are committed to the vitality and development of minority language communities throughout Canada. Let us build respect and understanding between our two great language communities, not division and conflict.
April 1, 1993

Mr. Speaker, I find it extremely gratifying to draw your attention to a truly exceptional event I attended last week in my riding. More than 680 people came to show their gratitude and respect to more than 40 persons who received the Governor General's 125th anniversary medal, in recognition of their volunteer work and their involvement in the economic and socio-cultural activities of their community.
I want to take this opportunity to express my admiration and to thank these residents of Richmond-Wolfe.

Mr. Speaker, at the Clinton-Yeltsin summit this week the Prime Minister will announce, in his words, a considerable Russian aid package. The package will address most appropriately wheat shipments and technical assistance.
If Russia is to enjoy economic revitalization we must also support elements essential to industrial growth. One crucial area of unlimited potential is Russian oil and gas reserves.
Many Canadian companies have been negotiating contracts but due to political instability and lack of capital funding the deals are not finalized. One example, Algoma Steel of Sault Ste. Marie, a $50 million seamless tube order was announced by the Prime Minister, signed by our minister of trade and Russia's finance minister. A year later there is still no deal.
A positive development could be the expanded mandate of the Export Development Corporation which will allow it to become more involved in these deals. An example is to take on equity shares in projects.
Oral Questions
I ask the Prime Minister to take this weekend's opportunity to finalize any pending Russian-Canadian contracts which will be mutually beneficial.

Mr. Speaker, the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board has released its report which says that Canadian drug prices are among the highest of those with which Canada was compared.
During the passing of Bill C-91, known as the drug patent legislation, the opposition argued that it was our generic drug industry and compulsory licensing that kept our prices lower. So much for that argument. Similarly the price of Canadian prescription drugs was supposed to be lower because in Canada we had only 20 years of patent protection and any change would make us pay more.
The Liberals are wrong again. Those countries that we were compared with in Europe have an average of 24 years of protection while in the U.S. they have an average of 25 years. Thus increasing the lifetime of a patent does not increase the price and in fact the opposite may be the reality.
The questions remain then: Has the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board been incapable in the past of controlling the price of prescription drugs and will the new powers given to the board because of Bill C-91 correct this apparent imbalance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
When the government proposed Bill C-91 we were told that drug prices would not increase for prescription drugs. Now a study confirms that Canada has some of the highest prices in the world.
I would like to know from the Prime Minister if it is true that the government proposed Bill C-91 to please the Bush administration during the NAFTA negotiations, as it was alleged yesterday by the senior senator

April 1, 1993
Oral Questions
of Arkansas who said that the government caved in under pressure from the Bush administration.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the statement by the senator mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition. However, his question does come as something of a surprise, when I consider that his party and he himself voted against Bill C-91, which would, among other things, give the board additional powers.
If he had voted for Bill C-91, the board would have had additional powers more quickly to monitor the price of drugs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister did not answer my question.
We want to know why this government always sides with the big multinationals instead of taking care of people who need drugs in this country, the poor and the sick. When will this government make it a priority to look after the weakest members of our society instead of siding with the multinationals who contribute to the coffers of the Conservative Party?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is easy to be negative; however the hon. member forgot to mention the investments made in Quebec. He also forgot to mention the position of the Quebec government, something the hon. member does quite often. Investments that are being made thanks to Bill C-22 in 1987 and Bill C-91 today will ensure that research and development in the pharmaceutical sector takes place in Canada. That is good for Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot justify that the poor in our society, the sick in our society, have to pay these high prices which are higher than anywhere else in the world according to a report from his own department.
When will the government realize that a lot of those costs are paid by the provincial governments and the federal government and at this time the country cannot
afford to deduct big sums of money for the big international corporations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again, the hon. member overlooked something. He forgot that Bill C-91 applies to one category of drugs. He forgot to say that 80 per cent of the drugs used in this country have absolutely no connection with the legislation contained in Bill C-91, which was passed by the House.
Canadians will not be affected, although the Leader of the Opposition contends they will be, by a bill that, I repeat, will put Canada on the map as a good place to invest in the pharmaceutical sector, where we take a leading position.
Not so long ago, an article stressed how important it was for Canada to have this special niche in research and development with respect to Canadian pharmaceutical products.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of health.
Yesterday the minister of health claimed in the House that the government's policies have led to lower drug prices for Canadians. One of the government's own departments obviously disagrees with him.
In a letter sent to all Canadian veterans the department says: "In recent years the cost of health care benefits has risen sharply. The cost of prescription drugs has been one of the main reasons for this increase".
Yesterday the minister dismissed the findings of the regulatory agency, the PMPRB. I want to ask the minister if today he will stand in his place and accept the findings of one of his own departments, the Department of Veterans Affairs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, the hon. member's question is much the same as the previous one. However, he failed to mention that it is important to have this board, which has the power it needs to review what is happening here in Canada. I would like to state more specifically the additional fines that can be imposed and the fact that the board may
April 1, 1993

review whatever is going on with respect to pharmaceutical products in this country.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
I will give the minister one more chance. Green Shields, a private insurer, the province of Ontario, the province of British Columbia, the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board, and now the Department of Veterans Affairs are telling the government that its drug patent policy simply does not work for Canadians.
I want to ask the minister if he will finally wake up and realize that the policy he has been pursuing is not for the benefit of Canadians. It has been solely for the benefit of international pharmaceutical companies.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if $500 million worth of investment in Canada does not benefit Canadians, I wonder what the hon. member expects and what he sees as benefiting Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I too have a memo from Veterans Affairs Canada in which Veterans Affairs Canada writes to veterans.
In recent years, the cost of health care benefits has risen sharply. The cost of prescription drugs has been one of the reasons for this increase. The challenge for Veterans Affairs is to continue meeting your health needs at a reasonable cost. One way to do this is by filling your drug prescriptions with lower-priced generic drug products.
Yesterday when I asked this question of the minister in the House, he told me:
We have no intention of conducting an investigation into the price of drugs, since we have the appropriate mechanisms to ensure that prices remain at reasonable levels for Canadian users.
I want to say to the minister responsible that here is further evidence that drug prices are hurting Canadians. They are hurting veterans. The government's own departments recognize it. Will the government reconsider and hold an inquiry into high drug prices in Canada?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has taken the necessary steps to ensure two things: First, that pharmaceutical industries come and operate in Canada- which is good for the country in terms of investments- and second, that a board be put in place to make sure that patented medicines are sold in Canada at a justifiable cost.
Bill C-91 gave more powers to the board, thereby guaranteeing that patented medicines would be sold at a reasonable price.
Therefore, I think that the hon. member's question is irrelevant.

A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. Since its creation five years ago, the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board has initiated only one inquiry. One inquiry in five years is not what I would call an efficient way of monitoring prices. Drug prices in this country are 56 per cent above the international average. This is hurting senior citizens and chronic care patients who have to pay. Please, launch a ministerial inquiry.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what my colleague is forgetting when comparing Canada with other countries is that those countries do not necessarily have generic products and might have longer patent protection than the one we have recently had under the new legislation.
If I follow her reasoning, Bill C-91 should have given even longer patent protection to innovative companies.

Mr. Speaker, the government's own Department of Veterans Affairs acknowledges that generic drugs are lower priced and urges clients to get lower priced generic drugs.
The cost to Canada of this awful legislation is tremendous. I just want to say to the government that we are asking Canadians to expect less and less in health care. Ontario estimates it could lose $100 million because of this legislation. Saskatchewan and Manitoba could lose $10 million a year and New Brunswick almost $15 million a year.

April 1, 1993
Oral Questions
I want to say, while we are asking Canadians to take less and less and we are giving to multinational corporations, surely the government has a responsibility to stand and have an inquiry into high drug prices in Canada. Will it do it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Vincent (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer is yes, the Government of Canada has a responsibility and that is making sure that research and development is carried out in the pharmaceutical industry in this country. We need research and development activity in that field, and our government acted accordingly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House have been asking repeatedly for many months questions of the government to provide all of the documents, including the censored documents, in order to shed light on the facts surrounding the Westray coal mine disaster.
I have in my hand a letter addressed to me signed by Justice Peter Richard, wherein he states: "The order was served on the Government of Canada with notice to the Minister of Justice through an associate deputy minister. I was assured by the associate deputy minister that the federal government would co-operate with the inquiry".
I ask the right hon. Prime Minister if he would indicate to the House whether or not the then Minister of Justice was acting alone or acting in full concert and knowledge of the entire cabinet.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member raises questions about this government co-operating with the provincial commission of inquiry.
He knows that we have co-operated right from the beginning, over 7,500 pages worth of documents. We will be tabling further documents with the commission. We have co-operated with them from the beginning to the end.
The previous Liberal government never co-operated with provincial inquiries. We are.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is clear from the response of the minister that not only was there no co-operation forthcoming, but the Government of Canada has deliberately withheld information, censored documents from the judicial inquiry and from the Parliament of Canada.
Yesterday the minister made mention in this House repeatedly about the families of the deceased miners. I have in my hand a letter from a brother of a deceased miner who states in a letter written December 2, 1992 and I quote: "Quashing inquiries and protecting the rights of those responsible only reinforce the prevailing opinion of a massive cover-up. We will not let the federal or provincial governments steamroller us on this one".
I again ask the right hon. Prime Minister: Was the then former Minister of Justice acting alone or with the full consent and knowledge of the entire cabinet? Yes or no.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said yesterday, and I am going to have to say it again, the only cover-up that has existed with regard to this matter is the hon. member who comes in here with documents that he has had for three or four months which he says purport to reflect on why these miners died, and he does not table them before the House and he did not tell the House about them until two days ago.
I want to give my hon. friend three pieces of information that he should listen to very carefully. First of all, the CANMET report which he said had not been tabled with the commission was tabled with the commission six months ago and the commission counsel confirmed that two days ago; no apology from the hon. member for alleging otherwise.
April 1, 1993

There was an additional red herring. They said: "No, there are seven pages missing from the CANMET report". I received a letter from our counsel to the commission counsel confirming this morning that there are no missing seven pages. The CANMET report was nine pages yesterday, the day before, forever. It is still nine pages.
The third particular matter which I think the hon. member should understand is that we want to co-operate with the commission because we want to get to the bottom of why these miners died. Safety being a provincial jurisdiction it is properly the purview of a provincial commission. We are happy to co-operate with them.
Here is what Mr. John P. Merritt, the commission counsel, said late yesterday in a letter that I received from the government's counsel. He said: "All information which may be received or gathered by the commission staff during the period that criminal charges are outstanding will be kept confidential by the commission and not be released".
He has also said: "Parties with status will have access to that information once any risk of jeopardizing the criminal proceedings has been removed".
We are concerned about the criminal proceedings, about the RCMP inquiry. Because of that we were very concerned that tabling documents with the commission that were not confidential could impede that inquiry.
We are satisfied with this letter from John Merritt, the commission counsel. I asked my officials, pursuant to this letter that we received late yesterday giving us assurance to speak to the commission, to contact them so that we can transfer these documents most convenient to them as soon as possible at a time appropriate for them.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The minister who has just answered talked about everything but the question that was put by the opposition House leader. I want to quote again from the letter written by Justice Richard to the opposition House leader in which he says: "The order was served on the Government of Canada with notice to the Minister of Justice through an associate deputy minister. I was
Oral Questions
assured by that associate deputy minister that the federal government would co-operate with the inquiry".
The federal government has not co-operated with the inquiry. Evidence has not been forthcoming.
I want to ask the Prime Minister as the chief of cabinet whether or not the then Minister of Justice was acting alone when she withheld the necessary evidence from a judicial commission of inquiry, or was she acting with the knowledge and consent of cabinet, including the Prime Minister?

Mr. Speaker, the suggestion that a minister, the then Minister of Justice, withheld information either from the cabinet or from the commission of inquiry is of course false, misleading and should be withdrawn on the floor of the House of Commons by the hon. member.
Second, in regard to-
Why? She withheld it.

Well now the member from Winnipeg is making an even more serious accusation. He is saying that the Minister of Justice knowingly withheld information from an inquiry, presumably with the view to undermining the integrity of that inquiry. That is very serious.
Have we got under your skin?
If my hon. friend wants to make that charge-
Just a minute. It might be easier if all hon. members listened to the question and then listened to the answer. The right hon. Prime Minister has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I am merely indicating, as the minister indicated, that the government has co-operated fully with the inquiry.
I am not acquainted with the particular correspondence that was cited by my hon. friend a few moments ago, and he may care to table it, from the chief justice or the justice who chairs the inquiry. Once we find out when that was sent and what it says we will take a look at

April 1, 1993
Oral Questions
it. If there is any difficulty I or the minister will be happy to clarify any difficulties that may arise.
The allegation that has been made seems to be clearly a concerted one coming from the Official Opposition, directed against the former Minister of Justice, and suggesting that she deliberately conspired with someone to withhold information from a judicial inquiry. That is a very serious accusation.
Normally in this Parliament if you make that kind of accusation you rise and you put your seat in play and if you are wrong, resign.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister knows and it is an acknowledged fact that the counsel for a judicial commission of inquiry took the extraordinary step of going public to rebut the assertion by the government House leader that all of the information that had been asked for had been received. That extraordinary measure was taken.
The government has acknowledged repeatedly that it is refusing under cabinet confidentiality terms to release 18 pages of documents including specifically a memo written to the minister of energy. That is all acknowledged fact.
What is now clear is that the request for information was conveyed to the Government of Canada through the office of the Minister of Justice.
The only question being asked of the Prime Minister is this: Was the then Minister of Justice acting alone or was the then Minister of Justice acting with the knowledge and consent of cabinet? Was this a cabinet decision to withhold from a judicial commission of inquiry the very evidence it sought to investigate this Westray coal mine disaster, Prime Minister? Yes or no.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He apologized for it.

speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: It is acknowledged fact.

Mr. Speaker, one day they are after the minister of defence for helicopters and then one day they are after the former Minister of Justice on something else.
Let us examine this. The member just made a statement about the commission counsel of the royal commission in Nova Scotia. It is my understanding that statement by my hon. friend is one that he ought to have
known had already been corrected by the commission counsel who apologized to the government. That information was conveyed to my hon. friend yesterday on the floor of the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Absolutely, absolutely.
No.
She made the statement, not us.

I am not going to yell back and forth across the floor at my hon. friend. It seems to me it is a simple proposition. Either the commission counsel in Nova Scotia apologized to the government and acknowledged he was wrong or he did not. If I am wrong in making that statement I will be happy to withdraw it but that is the information that I have received. That is the information that has been conveyed to the House.
It is wrong.

My hon. friend says I am wrong. If I am I will be happy to examine the documents again. The information that we have is that the commission counsel so acknowledged his error; that the government had responded fully to the requests that had been raised by the Official Opposition.
It's wrong. He didn't say that.

The second question raised by my hon. friend is in regard to the Minister of Justice. The question presumes and suggests that the Minister of Justice did something other than pursue her duties in an honourable and entirely appropriate way. Of course she did no such thing. She conducted herself at all times as Minister of Justice in a manner in keeping with the highest standards of the leading law officer of the Crown, which means that there was no such suggestion of any kind made by my hon. friend, and he would do well to withdraw that allegation right now.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Solicitor General.
The RCMP today stated that cigarette smuggling has now been taken over by organized crime. On Tbesday the minister of revenue admitted in the House that tobacco companies are not co-operating in preventing cigarette
April 1, 1993

smuggling and are in fact making it impossible for the RCMP to trace contraband cigarettes.
In view of these developments, will the minister now reimpose the $8 per carton export tax and cut the feet out from under organized crime?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can advise my hon. friend that although the job of the Solicitor General seems to cover a multitude of things it does not cover raising taxes, so I will skip that one, if he does not mind.
I would say that he raises a very important point. There is no question that the smuggling of cigarettes is a serious matter, one that the government views with a great deal of concern. We are presently consulting internally and with provinces in an effort to mount an offensive to stop the smuggling.

Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General was present when the export tax was removed and took part in the press conference so I thought he knew something about it.
I want to give the minister every opportunity to get tough with organized criminals smuggling cigarettes, even though this government caved in last year when the tobacco lobby came calling.
The RCMP now admits it is able to only intercept 5 per cent of smuggled cigarettes. What new measures is this government prepared to bring forward to assist the RCMP? That is within his jurisdiction.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no question that we are going to develop as many new methods of dealing with this matter as possible. I am not prepared to deal with them on the floor of the House of Commons until they are finalized. Until such time as they are finalized I am only going to lay out in public those matters which it makes sense to lay out in public. The rest of them we use to get the smugglers.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. Yesterday
Oral Questions
we were informed that the government was considering raising the pay of inmates in federal penitentiaries.
I thought this was too silly to get too concerned about, until I read the newspaper this morning and saw that the leprechaun Sean Durkan from The Toronto Sun had stated that this was indeed a fact, that we were going to raise the salaries of inmates in federal penitentiaries.

Given that some pages are missing from the document that the commission has, did the Minister of Justice hide documents with or without the consent of the Prime Minister and Cabinet?

How does it strengthen the Canadian base of that industry to close the productive, efficient and profitable Wyeth plant in Windsor and instead of creating more jobs, to eliminate 129 jobs altogether and to transfer the remaining 90 out of the city? What sense does that make?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. He recognizes our questions deal with the very important issue of public accountability and trust of members of the government.

there is anything inconsistent with what the justice said in respect of the government's obligations.
The government views this matter with extreme seriousness, as I am sure do all members of the House of Commons. There was loss of life involved.
There was the question of a judicial inquiry having been constituted by a duly elected provincial government to determine areas of responsibility. There has been involvement by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in respect of possible prosecutions that might ensue. There has been the intervention of an appellate court in this matter holding in abeyance evidence that might have been adduced before this particular royal commission.
There has been a full and ongoing degree of co-operation by the Government of Canada, given those realities to which I have just referred. The Minister of Justice, as she then was, and all ministers of the government have co-operated fully. If my hon. friend has something at variance with what I have just said I would be happy to listen to it, take a good look at it with him and make sure that the proper thing is done. Mr. Speaker, there was an editorial in The Chronicle-Herald this morning. We have had acknowledged in this House-

Given the time, could the hon. member put his question, please.

Mr. Speaker,
I am responding directly to the inquiry and to the Prime Minister.
Why is it that the Government of Canada, by the Minister of Justice or the collective entity of the cabinet, did not provide all the documents as requested last August and is still holding out on those documents today?

I just want to tell my hon. friend, Mr. Speaker, he is right in two areas. First, it is of course a very serious matter and the Chronicle-Herald is a very serious newspaper. I do not dismiss any views on this casually and we are going to co-operate very fully with the commission of inquiry.

showed that the cuts will result in lost tax revenue and increased UI payments for a net loss to the Treasury.

You doubled the debt.
Mr. Speaker, you cannot have it both ways. If you want to control the debt, you cannot spend yourself rich.

Mr. Speaker, the fact of the matter is this government doubled the debt. In its attempt to reduce the debt this study shows it has in fact increased the debt. That is the point of the study.
My supplementary is for the same minister. Today Time Warner Inc. will place on the news-stands the Canadian edition of Sports Illustrated. Time Warner is clearly circumventing Canadian customs and skimming scarce Canadian advertising dollars. It plans to publish six Canadians editions during the year, yet this government refuses to act until a task force reports at the end of the year.
Why will the government not show some backbone, seize the Canadian edition of Sports Illustrated and enforce the laws of the land?

April 1, 1993
Business of the House
Mr. Speaker, it is hard for me to see how that question was supplementary to the previous one, but I am glad to respond to it anyway.
You figure it out.

The hon. member says I should figure it out. Anybody looking at the two questions would have a hard time figuring it out.
In so far as Sports Illustrated is concerned, the policy of this government is to ensure that the letter of the law is followed fully. What we want to ensure is that the policy that was put in place in 1965 is respected. We have created the task force to look into this sort of issue. There is no requirement that the task force wait until the end of the year. Any time the task force is prepared to make an interim report or a final report, the government will be pleased to receive it.
Our goal is to ensure that the Canadian magazine industry is fully protected.

Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for the opportunity for me to make a comment.
It is highly appropriate in the discussion on this tax bill that we bring to mind the whole plight of the disabled and the income tax system. A report was done by the Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons. It brings forward the issue of taxation and the disabled because disability involves costs. There were some very specific recommendations made.
The Department of Finance, for one, should become a full and active partner in the national strategy for the integration of persons with disabilities. In relation to the costs and the reintegration of disabled people into mainstream economy and society, there were a number of specific recommendations made. I would like to cite three very briefly and ask my hon. colleague to comment on them.
The changes to the tax system should reflect the following principles:
First, that taxes that people with disability pay should be reduced by measures that offset all their disability-related costs.
Second, the tax system should be used as a delivery mechanism for benefits to lower income individuals with a disability. This relates to income reform as well.
Third, the tax system should be used to remove or reduce the disincentives for disabled people to join the work force.

April 1, 1993
Government Orders
This is a fairly major issue and concern for people who are basically impacted on by the constraints produced by a person's disability. All programs have a social component, including the income tax system, and should be designed to alleviate the disadvantage experienced by people with disabilities in an equitable and fair manner. Bear in mind that these programs should enhance the independence and particularly the employment opportunities for disabled people.
I would like to ask my hon. colleague how he feels about the support there for these recommendations. This is highly appropriate because the Association for Community Living for the Disabled is meeting in Ottawa. I am sure that they have had contacts with many hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague from Western Arctic for that question. Indeed I want to thank her particularly for raising some of the positive aspects in this bill.
She and I have discussed this aspect in advance of her question and I am very much aware of the ongoing work and the work of the committee that had made the recommendations. I want to add that we may recall that I reflected on the nine or ten separate aspects of the items that are included in this bill. This is essentially a bill that includes numerous technical amendments and changes to the Income Thx Act.
It is regrettable that these very positive aspects such as the recommendations made in this report, many of which are incorporated in the bill, are overcome by some of the negative aspects of the bill with respect to essentially opening loopholes for the rich when it should be closing loopholes for Canada's most wealthy. The other somewhat inconsistent and I believe shameful aspect of the bill is that it does not permit the kind of privacy that we, in a Canadian society, would want for employees. These are the 20,000 members of the Public Service who are involved with Revenue Canada.
As a finale statement to this and on a personal note I want to tell the hon. member that for many years I have been a director of the Canadian Paraplegic Association and have worked with the community living movement which is a very important movement in my riding. That was the point that she made at the very beginning. It gives me great personal satisfaction to see that the
disabled are considered in this bill. In my opinion I think the plight of the disabled is one of the most positive aspects of the bill. This is in response to the tremendous bootstrap work that they are doing in the Canadian Paraplegic Association and the Institute for the Blind, which has been in the public eye in the last few days, and other areas of community living. Again I would also say that I believe they are making great strides and this is another indication of that. Therefore I thank the hon. member for her question. I was pleased to be able to highlight that positive aspect of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that I am able to enter third reading stage debate on Bill C-92. It is an omnibus bill. I am only going to confine my remarks though to one part of it, the part dealing with the extension of the capital gains exemption for principally the very rich and the very powerful families of this country.
I think it is an absolute disgrace for this government or indeed any government at this time. We are in the depths of a recession. Middle income earners have been overburdened with tax increases for the past several years. User fees are going up. Provincial taxes are going up. Deficits are ballooning out of sight. There are poor, hard-working, middle income earners. There are those households where incomes are around $40,000 to $50,000 a year if they are lucky and two persons are working in that family. Now this Conservative government has to bring in an amendment to the Income Tax Act that would further exempt family trusts for up to another 75 or 80 years.
The history to this family trust debacle in this country goes back to 1972 when the then Liberal government decided to bring to an end succession duties and estate taxes, particularly estate taxes at the federal level. In place of the estate taxes they introduced a system of taxes on capital gains which hitherto had gone untaxed. At that time of course that was looked upon as being unfair as well.
In place of the estate tax, and when they brought on the capital gains tax in 1972, the government of that day-I was here in the House of Commons at that time-brought in the 21-year rule which said that family trusts would have up to 21 years in order to prepare for a capital gains tax on their private family estates. Most of them, believe me, took advantage of it.
April 1, 1993

Contrary to the impression left by some Conservative speakers in this debate, this family trust is not your ordinary, run of the mill kind of legal and financial arrangement that your average taxi driver engages in or that your average nursing assistant has or that your average truck driver is able to afford. For one thing, to set up a family trust costs several thousands of dollars so automatically most ordinary taxpayers of middle-income status are unable to set up a family trust.
Second, most families in this country, the great majority of them, have no financial reason to set up a family trust. They simply do not have assets large enough to warrant that kind of expenditure or legal cost that is required to set up the family trust.
What we are really talking about here is primarily, not exclusively, the very rich in this country. We are talking, for example, about the K.C. Irvings, the Reichmanns, the Bronfmans, the Westons, the Thomsons, the Rogers and the Blacks. We are talking about very, very rich and powerful families that have been able to shelter or avoid paying capital gains on their family wealth for 21 years.
This government through Bill C-92 has decided to let them go for another, as I said earlier, 75 or 80 years. It now says that when the capital gain is sold, it will not be taxed until the last beneficiary dies. Today, if I was very rich and I left the whole family trust to a child just bom this week, the chances of that child living to be 75 or 80 is very great in this modem age in which we live, so in effect the capital gain accumulating over the years on that family trust will go untaxed for another 75 or 80 years.
What kind of a message is this sending to the middle income earner, to the low income earner, to people out there who are trying to make ends meet?
Since 1984 this government has increased just federal taxes alone on average Canadians by about $3,000 a year. Because it has off-loaded much of its financial responsibilities and deficit on to the provinces by cutting back the rate of increase in transfers, the Canada Assistance Plan and other financial devices or mechanisms that it has established over the years by which it sends or transfers funds to the provinces, it will just cut back on the increase caused by inflation over the past few years. The provinces are now having to cut back very drastically.
Government Orders
We see it in the province of Newfoundland. We saw it just this week in the province of New Brunswick. In Saskatchewan, after eight years of profligate Conservative spending in that province, the NDP government has had to slash expenditures, cut back on programs, having to borrow more money and in a very dire deficit situation.
British Columbia is not as badly off, but there are also cutbacks there I understand. The province of Ontario I suppose is the best example of all. It came into office in September 1990 with a ready-made deficit of $5 billion. Because of declining revenues due to the recession that was setting in at that time and also the profligate spending again, this time not a Conservative government but a Liberal government under David Peterson, which presided over Queen's Park during the five richest years of Ontario's history, Ontario still managed to come up with a deficit of half a billion dollars in the treasury.
Because of all these changes and because today civil servants are threatened with their jobs or pay freezes or cutbacks in wages and private sector employees have lost their jobs to a great extent-there are 400,000 or 500,000 jobs that have gone down the tube as a result of restructuring and the free trade agreement-and companies are going bankrupt, because of all of these reasons, private sector and public sector employees are finding it extremely difficult to cope with taxation and increased user fees and the cutback on government services at all levels, federal, provincial and municipal.
We then have to contend with this kind of easy soft treatment that this Conservative government is now offering the richest 200 or 300 families in this country whose combined total assets are in the neighbourhood of about $70 billion. We are not talking about hundreds of thousands of families here. We are talking about, relatively speaking, a very small number of rich and powerful families in this country that can yet again defer capital gains tax on their family trusts for another 75, 80 or 85 years.
This is an intolerable situation. How can a government on the one hand talk about restraint and cutting back on government expenditures and on the other hand increase taxes to ordinary Canadians and then let the very rich and the very powerful off the tax hook as far as their family trusts are concerned?

April 1, 1993
Government Orders
It just does not make any sense. Worse than that, it sends a signal to ordinary Canadians that this government does not care a dam about equity and fairness in the tax system, but will continue to protect those few rich families in this country who, probably without exception, support the Conservative Party either directly through funding or certainly at the ballot box.
Many, many people have made comments about the unfairness of Bill C-92 as it affects family trusts. It is not just members of the New Democratic Party who are opposed to it, it is not just labour, it is not just anti-poverty groups, but many professional institutions and professional people have also made comments. For example, Sidney Goldstein of Goldstein and Goldstein in Ottawa, who is a tax lawyer and consultant, says and I quote: "There is no question that it"-that is Bill C-92-"represents a massive windfall for existing trusts".
Why would a person with his knowledge and with his experience-he is not only a lawyer but he is also a tax consultant and tax expert-make a statement like that if it were not true? I doubt very much that he is a supporter of the New Democratic Party.
It is not just us here on this side of the House who are condemning this as an unfair and inequitable approach to an over-all fair taxation system that we are desperately trying to bring in in this country.
Kathryn Bush of Blake, Cassels & Graydon had this to say and I quote: "A cynical person might suggest that pressure from influential political supporters also should be listed as a reason for the draft legislation". This is when she was commenting on the original legislation when it was first drafted. It has not changed in respect of family trusts since then.
Neil Brooks, associate dean of Osgoode Hall Law School, said and I quote: "The government has given Canada's wealthiest families notice that it intends to give them a gift worth several billions of dollars".

that this is a gift, a handout to the very rich people in this country. At the same time this government purports to have a deep sympathy for the hard working middle income earner who pays the bills, abides by the law and tries to look after his family. That is a mythology.
I just read a book by an American Republican, Kevin Phillips, a political analyst, called Boiling Point. It is a book which I suggest every Conservative should read. In that book he explains how Governor Clinton of Arkansas was able to overthrow President George Bush in the presidential elections of last November.
In that book he describes how Bush's predecessor, Ronald Reagan, the great communicator, was able through his eight years, two administrations, from 1981 to 1988 to constantly remind the hard-working middle income earner in the United States, the industrial worker, the truck driver, the taxi cab owner and operator and so on that the reason their taxes were going up was because those profligate states and those profligate welfare agencies and those profligate municipal governments all over the United States were spending more and more of their hard earned tax dollars to pay the welfare rolls for the lazy who would not work. As long as Ronald Reagan could keep the hard working middle-income earner convinced that that was why his taxes were going up and he was continuing to slide from middle class into poverty in many cases, the industrial middle class continued to support Reagan as they had done probably for the first time in the presidential elections of 1980.
When fumbling George Bush came along and discovered all of a sudden that he could not communicate quite as well as his mentor Ronald Reagan, the situation began to change and Governor Clinton and his brain trust who helped him run his campaign brought in a whole new set of statistics and figures and facts.
To make a long story short, they were able to show through those two successive income tax reform regimes under Ronald Reagan and George Bush that it was not the low income or welfare recipients who were causing the middle class to have to pay higher taxes and user fees at the federal, state and municipal levels. Rather it was because the Republicans had actually lowered the effective taxes that the very rich in the United States had to pay. Therefore he was able to cast the eyes of the middle

class away from the poor and the helpless upward to the very rich and the powerful.
That sealed George Bush's doom. The middle class went back to the Democratic Party convinced it was not the poor who were dragging them into poverty but the fact that the rich were in a privileged tax position in the United States and they were not paying their fair share.
We can use the identical argument in this country because that is precisely what has been happening in Canada since this Conservative government, like its Republican cousins in the United States, took power.
If we look at the national debt in this country, we find that 50 per cent of that national debt increases as the result of compounded interest. Forty-four per cent of that debt is caused by tax avoidance. That is a legal term I know and I do not mean it in a legal sense. They are not doing things that are illegal, but the very rich families in this country at the personal income tax level and the very rich corporations all through the 1980s, and I am not talking about the recession years of 1991-92,1 am talking about all through the 1980s, were not paying their fair share of taxes. Mr. Speaker, the debate on Bill C-92 is drawing to a close, and I have only five minutes to provide a summary of this bill. Since the legislation itself is far too complex to explain in a few minutes, I will concentrate on the important principles we should observe when governing a country with a population of over 27 million people.
First of all, what is essential in a democracy is the way we tax our citizens and ourselves. Nothing could be more basic. The way we are taxed and tax others should be fair and equitable, irrespective of the taxpayer's position in society. This is an important principle of democracy and responsible government, which we have inherited and which goes back for centuries. It has evolved over time, but the ultimate goal remains the well-being of our fellow citizens.

Government Orders
What has happened recently? We had the so-called tax reform. I know they used the word "reform", but that is not necessarily what it means. We had tax increases, but the burden of those increases was felt to a far greater extent by the middle class than by the wealthiest segment of our society. These increases came in the form of indirect taxes, consumer taxes and, finally, the GST, a tax that has created so much frustration for entrepreneurs and retailers in this country. Even today, two years later, there is still a general feeling of frustration as a result of this tax.
Reform was the order of the day. They introduced the GST, and gradually people are realizing that the GST did not deliver the expected results. People predicted there would be serious problems but they went ahead anyway. Today, the figures are coming out at various committees mentioned by the hon. member from Ottawa: a certain amount was collected by the government which had to use part of it to finance operations. Rebates had to be paid as well. All this goes to show that the net benefit of all these taxes leaves a lot to be desired.
However, what I find particularly interesting in Bill C-92, after talking about the fairness principle and the need to have a tax that is fair and equitable, is the part that deals with family trusts. Bill C-92 contains a truly bizarre provision which defies justification and flies in the face of the principle of tax equity. Twenty-one years ago the Liberal government at the time introduced amendments to the family trust provisions. It decided to adopt the 21-year rule, in other words, irrespective of the type of family trust, after 21 years the accrued value of these trusts would be taxed. It was a way to get rid of this tax shelter for the country's wealthiest families. On January 1, 1993 all trusts were obliged to pay the taxes which had accrued during those years.
The bill provides that the 21-year rule will no longer apply and that family trusts will be taxed only after the youngest member has died. In some cases this may take 20, 30 or even more than 40 years. So this is another substantial benefit.
Experts and tax lawyers appearing before the parliamentary committee argued that it was a tremendous advantage for the wealthiest families in our country.
Where is the fairness and justice in all this? I would say that of all the tax bills that have been passed in this House, this is the worst.
I think this is a disgrace. When we form the government this fall, our first responsibility will be to rescind this bill and apply the 21-year rule.

He said: Madam Speaker, I am most pleased to rise today and speak to this motion. There are very few subjects on which I have received so much correspondence and promotion other than this one since I have been elected.
There are a large number of people in Canada who have been trying to deal with this health related issue for a number of years. Unfortunately, to this date they have not been successful.
I want to pay tribute to some of them because their perseverance has ensured that this matter be debated within the House of Commons. People like Jack Newman in Toronto, Renee Hefti in Vancouver, Jean Geary and Elisabeth Sterken have kept this issue alive in spite of the opposition from the rather large lobbies within the infant formula companies.
Much to my amazement within the last three days when it became known that this bill was going to be discussed this afternoon, I received a number of faxes from right across Canada supporting this motion. They were from health organizations, health workers, paediatricians, nurses and others who have become interested in the whole issue of breast-milk substitutes.

April 1, 1993
Private Members' Business
I want to discuss the subject by laying out three or four areas. First, why should we be promoting breast-feeding? Second, what is the international code? Third, what has been the voluntary code that the companies claim they have been following in Canada? Fourth, what in fact is actually happening in this country?
Breast feeding is a serious health matter. We are more and more switching our concept of health to preventive health. Preventive health means that we ensure how we practise our lifestyles promotes the optimum health in people.
Information is now increasingly being accumulated that shows breast feeding has significant health improvements for infants. Breast-fed infants experience lower gastrointestinal disease rates and reduced respiratory illness. The ratios are quite striking.
There is an incidence of four to six times more gastrointestinal infections in bottle-fed infants. Respiratory illnesses are five times as high. There is indication that breast feeding reduces the incidence of bacterial meningitis.
There is some interesting information being accumulated which shows that bottle-fed babies have an increased risk of insulin dependence. Lymphomas are six times more common in babies who have not been breast fed.
We have a whole series of medical reasons as to why infants should be breast fed. There are benefits to the mother. There are medical reports that indicate there is a reduced incidence of breast cancer and ovarian cancer in women who breast feed babies. Not only is it medically beneficial to the infant it is medically beneficial to the mother.
There are also economic reasons for breast feeding. Right now the cost of infant formulas or breast-milk substitutes range anywhere from $1,200 to $3,000 a year. When you start looking at a mother who is on a low income, this represents a significant expenditure. It is particularly significant for women who are living on income assistance or women who are supporting themselves on one income, so we have an economic reason for breast feeding also.
Most literature certainly indicates that infants should be breast fed for as long as possible, six months to a year.
Right now between 20 per cent and 25 per cent of babies are basically fed on formula only. Some reports indicate that 50 per cent of mothers stop nursing within three months.
If there is a medical reason or it is not possible for the mother to nurse that is one thing, but what we have is the infant formula companies convincing women that they should not nurse, that there are better ways of feeding their infants.
I hope the parliamentary secretary to the minister of health who seems to defend the big multinational infant formula companies will speak on this bill and will explain why the government is tolerating the kind of marketing practices that are taking place by the companies.
There is a World Health Organization code that has been developed to set a code as to what the marketing practices for breast-milk substitutes should be. The code is fairly detailed. I would like to read just the summary of the 10 major points: "There shall be no advertising of these products to the public, no free samples to mothers, no promotion of products in health care facilities, no company mothercraft nurses to advise mothers, no gifts or personal samples to health workers, no words or pictures idealizing artificial feeding, including pictures of infants on the labels of the products. Information to health workers should be scientific and factual. All information on artificial infant feeding including the labelling should explain the benefits of breast feeding and the costs and hazards associated with artificial feeding." There are other parts to the code but those are the significant ones that I want to spend my time addressing this afternoon.
The industry decided it would adopt a voluntary code of practice for the Canadian Infant Formula Association. I want to read some of the things it said it would do voluntarily. Its code is quite extensive but I will just read a few of the points.
It says: "Member companies recognize that the decision to breast feed or not to breast feed, to discontinue breast feeding or to supplement breast feeding should be made by mothers with the counsel and advice of other health professionals and infant formula companies should not be involved in such decisions. Product claims will only contain statements that are consistent with sound medical and scientific data".

It goes on: "Infant formula companies will not make grants or contributions to support research, educational programs, fellowships, participation in professional meetings or the like or provide incidental services or professional courtesies for the purpose of discouraging breast feeding or encouraging hospitals or health care institutions to favour the donor's infant formula products and related products".
They will not make donations in order to encourage hospitals or health care institutions to favour the donor's infant formula products or related products. The donating company will inform the beneficiary institution such grants or contributions are made free, gratis, without any commercial conditions.
There are other things. It says that: "Samples of infant formula products will be provided only to medical facilities and health professionals for their discretionary distribution to mothers".
All of these things they glowingly say they are going to do. Let us look at what the major producers of infant formula are doing in Canada. I have pages of information where they simply totally disregard their own code, let alone the much more strenuous World Health Organization code.
I want to talk about them in three general areas. First of all, they give out misleading information. I have some examples where they say: "Just what the breast-feeding mother ordered". This is what they give to mothers directly: "Congratulations. Ross Laboratories joins you and your doctor, nurse and hospital extending to you, your baby and family the best wishes and good health and happy new year", just what the breast-feeding mother ordered. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I truly appreciate this opportunity to say some remarks with regard to the motion before the House. I have four youngsters and indeed did nurse four youngsters.
I have to say that when I took a set of twins home from the hospital and nursed both babies three hours apart, then I was very glad to have some formula around, thank you.
What my colleague is bringing forward has to do with a health issue and it affects every new mother, there is no doubt about it, and every baby around the world and I certainly concede to that.
For many years Health and Welfare Canada has been instrumental in promoting breast feeding as an ideal and the most preferred form of nourishing babies. Since 1985 Health and Welfare Canada has encouraged all hospitals to adopt policies and to adopt practices in support of breast feeding and of the international code of marketing of breast-milk substitutes adopted by the World Health Organization.
The government as well has encouraged the industry that produces and distributes infant formula in Canada to carry out self-regulation. The industry through the Canadian Infant Formula Association has adopted a code of practice that supports the aim and the principles of the international code of marketing of breast-milk substitutes.
The declared purpose of the code of practice is to ensure that the marketing practices of Canadian manufacturers of infant formula support Canada's national goal to promote breast feeding and ensure safe and adequate nutrition for all infants.
The first sentence of the code of practice declares that breast feeding is the preferred way of feeding most infants. The code of practice goes on to describe many

commitments, prohibitions and limitations on marketing practices.
Such detailed information on the claims of infant formula products will be directed only to the physician, so what they advertise goes only to physicians or other health professionals. Communication with scientific organizations and government agencies assures that marketing is in concert with their efforts to promote breast feeding, infant health and well-being.
This motion now before the House proposes that the government adopt as binding in Canada the international code of marketing of breast-milk substitutes issued by the World Health Organization. If one looks at the universal scope of this code and some of the provisions, they are neither applicable nor appropriate for implementation in Canada.
The code calls on member states to give effect to its principles and aim in the form they deem appropriate.
Canada has already done this through policies and practices which are appropriate and comprehensive. More than 10 years ago, after the adoption of the code by the World Health Organization, our Government of Canada obtained unanimous support for the aim and the principles of the code by all the provincial governments. The governments agreed that in Canada the code should be implemented not through legislation-this is all the 10 provinces plus the federal government-and regulation but through education, health promotion and co-operation.
Almost 80 per cent of the mothers in Canada start by breast feeding their babies and more than 40 per cent continue to breast feed their babies for at least three months. Health and Welfare Canada has carried out and will continue to carry out comprehensive programs that promote breast feeding such as the Breast Feeding Advocacy Kit, the National Guidelines on Family-Centred Maternity and Newborn Care, a publication called You and Your Baby and brochures such as Ten Great Reasons to Breast Feed and Ten Valuable Tips for Successful Breast Feeding.
In fact these efforts were underscored even further by the Minister of National Health and Welfare last year. He introduced an initiative called Brighter Futures that puts $500 million in new moneys for targeting areas of
Private Members' Business
concern with regard to youngsters up to seven years old. Brighter Futures recognizes the vital importance of breast feeding as a means of improving the health care of all infants.
Provincial governments continue in their partnerships with promoting programs. Non-governmental organizations throughout Canada and around the world continue their successful efforts to inform and educate parents on why breast feeding is by far the most beneficial way. Health professionals recognize and they know the effectiveness that their role has in promoting and supporting breast feeding.
This co-operative approach right across our country through the provincial governments, through all the agencies, and indeed with the federal government is serving mothers and children very well. Some people out there may ask: Who is making sure that our public policies, our national goals throughout this country and the international code are being followed. Why is there not legislation, as the hon. member across the way has asked? Why are there not regulations? Who is enforcing these codes?
I am sure that almost everybody in this House is aware that more legislation, more regulation and more policing is the last thing that we need. I think that the people of Canada as individuals are very responsible and they have to accept responsibilities, and indeed it is the woman's choice. Yes, she should be made aware of the benefits of breast feeding, but indeed the choice is hers. There are other implications that we do not know that may change her attitude. Indeed, it is up to the woman and her family with regard to breast milk.
Sure we have a code and a practice with the Canadian Infant Formula Association. As I said, we will work with all the provinces and we will not implement legislation. We will educate and make people aware and work with our provincial counterparts to make sure that the youngsters have the best.
