The child feels secure and loved.
What is the need for this motion? It is the aim of the World Health Organization in adopting the code to ensure that the slick advertising by infant formula manufacturers may not prompt mothers to buy formula rather than breast feed their babies. The importance of breast feeding cannot be over-emphasized.
In September 1991 the government acknowledged, as recorded in Hansard of the House of Commons, that it supported in principle the WHO international code. It said that it had played a key role in developing and promoting the code and that the department of health obtained unanimous support for the aim and principles of the code from all the Canadian provinces.
Furthermore, the government stated that it had taken a strong position with the Canadian infant formula industry by asking it to assume the responsibilities under the international code.
Things have happened differently. There have been many instances where mothers have been persuaded to start with the breast-milk formula because of the advertising approach and because formula is given free in the hospitals. That has been shown to in fact be a very persuasive tool.
If in fact this government is committed to this code, why does it not carry it to the logical conclusion and enshrine it into law, in legislation and regulation to prove its sincerity? Why not do it all: education, health promotion and a governing regulation and legislation so that when there is an infraction of this code the necessary teeth are there to ensure that the health of our babies and the health of our mothers are protected? That is the minimum that we can do for the health and welfare of mothers and babies in this country.
A headline recently published in The Montreal Gazette dated March 6,1993, read: "Hospital sold its soul for a $1 million grant". Dr. Haslam, president of the Canadian Paediatric Society, wrote and registered his protest to this approach. The Canadian Paediatric Society is the professional society that leads all paediatricians subscribing to the importance of breast feeding.
Breast feeding, as I said, is a natural and free product from a mother. The many medical advantages of human milk are known. It is known that breast-fed babies are not prone or are less prone to disturbances of the gastrointestinal tract. They have greater resistance to infection of the respiratory system. Breast feeding creates enhanced bonding between mother and child.
Just recently I spoke with Ms. Jean Geary of INFACT Canada who told me of her concerns as she had seen them in practice. There are no teeth in the voluntary compliance with the presently existing code in Canada. Breast feeding itself is not being protected. In fact, by the giving of free samples we are allowing those samples to be used immediately and that is known to inhibit lactation. She also told me that a video film has been produced by an infant formula company that will certainly downplay the role of breast feeding. All of these are counterproductive to the goal of ensuring that breast feeding is promoted in Canada.
I also spoke to Dr. Jack Newman of the University of Toronto Hospital for Sick Children, who is an expert in the field. He conveyed two messages to me. First, Canada has an obligation to adopt the international code. Since it has been acknowledged by the government that Canada has participated in a key way in the development of this international code, this code must be binding on all Canadian manufacturers of infant formula. This code must have teeth.
We should have regulation or enabling legislation in Canada to ensure that the intent and principle of the international code are followed in our country.
Dr. Newman related to me the many problems he had encountered in his clinical practice. Many babies become ill because of contaminated and improperly used formula. In fact, formula should be labelled as medication, just to be used only in certain circumstances. It should not be
April 1, 1993

the food of choice for infants. The milk product formula was never meant to be the food of choice. Breast milk ought to be the food of choice for all babies in our country.
On this note, I would like to lend my support to this motion. I hope the government will be challenged enough to adopt enabling legislation so that the intent and purposes of the international code are truly adopted in Canada without any doubt, with all the necessary safeguards and thereby ensure the health and welfare of our newborn Canadians and of our mothers.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for allowing me to speak to this motion.
I welcome the opportunity to discuss both our government's commitment to the principles of the international code and our concerted efforts to ensure that newborns in Canada benefit from the best available nutrition, their mother's milk.
All levels of care in Canada recognize and promote breast feeding as the preferred method of infant feeding, particularly in the first six months of life when infants are most vulnerable. The advantages of breast feeding include optimal infant nutrition, immunologic protection and psychological benefits.
Breast feeding had declined in many parts of the industrialized world including Canada. As a result, the promotion of breast feeding became a primary goal of the World Health Organization and Health and Welfare Canada.
In 1979, the World Health Organization and the United Nations Children's Fund proposed an international code governing the marketing of commercial infant formulas and other breast milk substitutes including bottle fed complementary foods.
Canada played a key role in developing the international code which is called the WHO International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes. The World Health Assembly passed the international code in May 1980.
Canada has also played a key role in promoting this important code. In 1981, the year after it was passed by the world health body, the Department of National Health and Welfare obtained unanimous support from all provinces for the aim and principles of the marketing code.
Private Members' Business
At that time the provinces endorsed using educational and health promotion initiatives to implement the code rather than using a legislative and a regulatory approach. The federal government continues to endorse this position. It also fosters an encouraging resurgence in popularity of breast feeding among new mothers.
Thirty years ago, only 38 per cent of the newborns in Canada were breast fed. By 1982 that number had nearly doubled reaching 70 per cent. Recent studies indicate that nearly 80 per cent of all newborns are now initially breast fed.
Comprehensive national health and welfare approaches which are also part of the code's recommendations are designed to increase awareness of the superiority of breast milk for the health of infants.
The department widely distributes a publication for new parents called You and Your Baby. It was formerly known as The Canadian Mother and Child. For years, this has promoted breast feeding as the preferred method of infant feeding.
Also two pamphlets for parents including Ten Great Reasons to Breast Feed, Ten Valuable Tips for Successful Breast Feeding and a breast feeding advocacy kit produced for health professionals and for the public encourage hospitals to adopt policies and practices in support of breast feeding and the WHO international code.
As well, the promotion of breast feeding is an integral part of the post-partum parent support program for the parents of newborns and for the family centred maternity and newborn care. These are national guidelines.
In recent years, the department has also worked closely with a variety of health professionals and advocacy groups to raise public awareness of the benefits of breast feeding. These efforts will continue with the government's commitment to children and to their families under the child development initiative of Brighter Futures.
Current objectives of breast feeding promotions are these and I would like to emphasize them: To increase the initiation and duration rates of breast feeding, thereby improving the health of infants and to encourage and support breast feeding as the culturally accepted norm in our communities.

April 1, 1993
Adjournment Debate
Moreover, the federal government recently reaffirmed its support for breast feeding as a contribution to children's help by signing the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. Signatories agree to ensure access in their countries to education about the advantages of breast feeding.
In addition, the composition and the production of infant formulas are strictly regulated under the Food and Drugs Act. Infant formula manufacturers must notify the Department of National Health and Welfare prior to making a major change in an existing formula or before introducing a new product.
Health and Welfare Canada has supported the selfregulation of the infant formula industry to ensure that the industry complies with the code's marketing objective. The department also promotes breast feeding to ensure that prospective parents and mothers of young infants are aware that the benefits of breast feeding to a child far outweigh the benefits of infant formulas.
As a result of negotiations with the Canadian Infant Formula Association, the infant formula industry agreed that education and advertising materials should not imply equivalence of the two sources of nutrition and should not discourage breast feeding. This is one of the basic principles of the international code of marketing of breast milk substitutes.
The industry also agrees to limit product promotion. The Canadian Infant Formula Association's own code stipulates that "infant formula companies will conform to the position of the Canadian Paediatric Society- which recommends that all advertising of infant formula products be directed to health professionals and not to the lay public".
Health and Welfare Canada encourages the infant formula industry in Canada to adhere to its voluntary commitment to the principle of the WHO code.
I will summarize by saying that the Department of National Health and Welfare will continue its co-ordination role in this important area, reflecting the federal government's policy of consultation and negotiation. Companies must provide information on a composition of the formula and submit the results of studies that demonstrate that the product will promote acceptable growth and development.

Mr. Speaker, on February 111 asked the Minister of Finance to cancel or postpone his announcement of December 2, 1992 to freeze grants in lieu of taxes paid to municipalities.
Many Canadians might ask: What are grants in lieu of taxes that are paid to municipalities? Prior to 1950 the Crown, that is the federal government, did not pay any taxes or grants to cities for their properties within those cities: post offices, airports, ports, office buildings and so on. It did not do so even though those federal buildings received services such as garbage collection, fire protection, snow removal, the roads and streets in the cities and so on. Those federal buildings received those services but until 1950 the federal government did not pay any city taxes.
In 1950 the federal government agreed that it should do so. Therefore it passed the Municipal Grants Act, which provided for grants in lieu of taxes to be paid to the cities. In that program there was a mechanism to adjust those taxes from year to year in accordance with the rates of inflation and increasing costs of the cities. The cities relied on that program as written and expected to get from year to year certain increases in those grants when there were increases in taxes.
April 1, 1993

On December 2 in the mini budget presented by the Minister of Finance he announced without any warning or consultation with the cities that he was freezing the grants to the cities in lieu of taxes at the 1992 level. He did that after many cities in Canada had already prepared their budgets for 1993.
They prepared their budgets on the basis of the agreements as they existed. As a result of that freeze the cities stand to lose approximately $80 million. The biggest loser of all the cities is the city of Montreal, my city, which will lose approximately $10 million.
A city like Montreal, having prepared its budget and having expected a certain amount of money from the federal government, now must scramble to deal with that unexpected loss. It will either have to further raise city taxes or cut out vital programs.
Some people may say that it should cut programs, but I do not think many would say that today if it was to cut out snow removal or garbage removal or whatever.
This is no way to run a country. Who else in this country can decide without any consultation or warning they are just not going to pay their taxes?
The reply from the minister to me on February 11 was that there were great increases in these grants in 1990, 1991, and 1992. He said that the amounts were very large.
That may be so, but those were large payments because they were based on the size and number of the federal government's buildings in those cities and the services that they received. The increases were based on cost of living increases and increased costs, so that is not an answer.
There may have been good grounds for the federal government to want to discuss with the cities revisions or changes in the program, but it should have done that. It should have proceeded with the discussions and then maybe after the discussions it could have arrived at a new program that would provide for lower payments if warranted. As I said, it went ahead and announced this freeze without any warning or any discussions with the cities.
I ask at least that the freeze be removed, or at the very least that it be postponed. I ask the parliamentary
Adjournment Debate
secretary once again to consider lifting the freeze or postponing it.

It would be useful to recall the purpose of the grants in lieu of taxes program. Under the Canadian Constitution, the federal government cannot be taxed by another level of government. However, the federal government has deliberately chosen to pay equivalent amounts in lieu of property taxes. We have paid property, and continue to pay, more than $400 million annually in grants, a very substantial contribution by any standards.
Over the past few years, grants in lieu of property taxes have increased at a rapid rate. For instance, in 1986-87, the total amount of grants in lieu of taxes on departmental property was $217 million. In 1992-93, this number almost doubled, rising to $424 million. During the past two years alone, grants in lieu of taxes have increased by more than 30 per cent. Considering the federal government's financial situation, that is clearly not sustainable.
The federal government is accountable to Canadian taxpayers. It must ensure that the payments it makes voluntarily are reasonable and appropriate, considering the equivalent tax rates they represent. After all, there is only one taxpayer.

Mr. Speaker, on March 17,1993 I said to the Minister of Employment and Immigration:
The immigration mail-in application system has been failing in Toronto for a year.
I spoke from 11 years of serving constituents in Trinity-Spadina, who are mostly foreign bom. Service by the immigration department has never been so bad, never been so careless, never been so negligent, and never been so contemptuous of the customer as it has been for the past year. That continues right up to April 1.
I also said, and this is the point:
MPs' inquiries often go unanswered for more than a month and too often the answer when it comes is there has been no officer working on that file for these months.
One example is a sponsorship that was undertaken on December 3, 1991. The constituent contacted this office in April 1992 and the office was told that there would be an answer by May 11, 1992. On May 26, 1992, the office was told that the file had not yet been processed and would probably be done in two months' time. In August the CIC said the application had not been looked at yet. "Someone is going to review original humanitarian and compassionate grounds, has not done it yet, not top priority".
By January 22, 1993 there was nothing on any answer from the Canada immigration service. On February 1 a call from the immigration service promised that the file would be taken care of. On March 9 in a call from the CIC it was indicated that the case file would be assigned to an officer. On March 15, 1993, there was a fax from the CIC and a call back to the CIC brought the information that it was not known who was in charge of the file for decision on H and C grounds.
Today, April 1, well over a year and a half after the application, the message the CIC sent was that the case file is with the assistant manager and our office should call back again in two weeks' time for further updating.
There is another ridiculous case. A lady applied to sponsor her mother in September 1991. The lady wrote to the CIC requesting an update and got no answer on the case. In December 1992, 15 months later, the CIC staff told my staff that the case was put into inventory and never looked at. They said it would be assigned to an officer with an urgent tag and if the constituent had not heard from immigration by January, the constituent should call. The constituent never heard from immigration. Two and a half years later, on February 22, 1993 a fax was sent to the immigration office requesting an update and there has been no answer as of April 1, today.
This is contemptuous behaviour toward the taxpayers who are paying the bills for this department.
My third and last example is a fax request to the department in December 1992 which was answered. This time I will have to admit it was answered later saying that they had faxed to the RCMP. The CIC had called back saying the RCMP reported that it was still outstanding. The update was requested December 4,1992 and was not back yet. Report 27 had to be written up on the client because of late extension of visa. Then, on March 13, a fax was sent after further conversations. It states: "This client is reportable under section 27 of the Immigration Act as she did not extend her visa in time. A report has to be written by an officer. To date the report is outstanding. We will transfer the file back to the officer dealing with this case".
They are simply contemptuous of the public who pay their fees, contemptuous of the members of Parliament who represent the public. They do not do the work because the staff has been so chopped, so reduced, so demoralized that it is impossible for them to carry out their duties. I ask the minister to cancel this stupid unworkable mail-in program.

Did he have his earmuffs on?

He must have, because I do not think he caught the urgency, the challenge, the crisis that exists. Net farm income works out to $5,000 for a family farm. An average family farm in Canada has a capital investment of $525,000. They have to have things like combines that cost $100,000.

The minister came to the committee meeting but he did not hear. He must have had his earmuffs on. The group was saying to him: There is a crisis out there.
